questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Open risks at project closure
questions.question: A ferry operator's online booking project is closing, and its project risk register holds three open security risks that will continue once the system is in operation. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Close the three risks in the project owner's register
options.B: Record the three risks in the lessons-learned report
options.C: Hand the risks to a business owner in the enterprise register
options.D: Ask the project owner to track the risks for another year

questions.key_concept: Project risks that continue into operation move to the enterprise risk register with an operational business owner when the project closes.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the risks end with the project or continue once the system runs.
questions.correct_explanation: Risks that outlast a project become operational risks, so they move into the enterprise register with an owner from the business that will run the booking system, where they are rated against appetite and monitored after the project team disbands. Having the project owner track them for another year is the runner-up: it keeps them visible for a while, but outside the enterprise register and only until the extra year ends.

wrong_explanations.A: Closing risks in the project owner's register is routine at closure; however, these risks continue in operation, and closing them leaves them with no owner or monitoring.
wrong_explanations.B: Lessons learned record what the project would do differently; however, they are not a risk record, so risks that continue in operation would have no owner or monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra tracking keeps the risks visible for a while; however, a project-side list sits outside the enterprise register, and the risks last beyond the extra year.

tips: Eliminate: A closes risks that continue in operation, and B files them as lessons learned, which no one owns or monitors.
Final two: C beats D because risks that continue in operation belong in the enterprise register with a business owner; a project-side list for a year sits outside the enterprise view.
Exam cue: at project closure, open risks that continue go to the enterprise register with a business owner; they do not close with the project.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. SaaS recovery gap
questions.question: A charity's SaaS donor database contract covers platform recovery but not restoring records that the charity's own users delete or corrupt. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reliance on the provider's platform recovery for donor records
options.B: A charity-managed backup of donor records sized to the RPO
options.C: A contract clause moving data-loss accountability to the provider
options.D: Training for charity users on deleting donor records

questions.key_concept: Under shared responsibility, the customer stays accountable for its data and covers the recovery the cloud contract leaves to it.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly which recovery the contract covers and which it leaves to the charity.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the shared responsibility model the contract sets who does what, and here restoring records the charity's own users delete or corrupt is left to it. Accountability for donor data stays with the charity whatever the contract says, so the gap is closed with a backup the charity controls, set by the data loss it can tolerate. A contract clause is the runner-up: it might shift some cost, but it cannot move accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: The provider's recovery protects the platform; however, the contract excludes restoring records the charity's users delete or corrupt, so relying on it leaves that loss unrecoverable.
wrong_explanations.C: Contract terms can shift cost or work; however, the charity stays accountable for its donor data, and a clause does not restore lost records.
wrong_explanations.D: Training can cut accidental deletions; however, it cannot bring back records once lost, and corruption can happen without any user mistake.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on recovery the contract excludes, and D lowers the chance of user error without making lost records recoverable.
Final two: B beats C because accountability for data cannot be contracted away; the charity closes its side of the gap with a backup it controls.
Exam cue: in the cloud, read what the contract leaves to the customer; the customer stays accountable for its data and covers its side of the shared model.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Test scenario versus top risk
questions.question: A bank's IT operations manager plans the yearly failover test of its core system; the bank's top-rated risk scenario is ransomware that also encrypts online backups. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Advance notice of the test date to staff
options.B: A yearly cycle for testing the online backups
options.C: A test scope limited to the core banking system
options.D: No test assuming the online backups are lost

questions.key_concept: Recovery tests are tied to the register's top scenarios; a test that never exercises the highest-rated scenario leaves recovery from it unproven.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the test assumes with what the top-rated scenario assumes.
questions.correct_explanation: Tests should prove recovery under the scenarios that matter most. The top-rated scenario assumes ransomware has encrypted the online backups, yet no test assumes they are lost, so the bank does not know whether it can recover from the event it rates highest. A narrow scope is the runner-up: covering more systems helps, but testing them the same way would still leave that scenario unproven.

wrong_explanations.A: Unannounced tests add realism; however, planned windows are normal for failover tests, and advance notice does not leave the top-rated scenario untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Test frequency follows risk and change; however, testing the online backups more often would still never prove recovery once ransomware has encrypted them.
wrong_explanations.C: A wider scope would help; however, adding systems tested the same way would still leave the bank's top-rated scenario unproven.

tips: Eliminate: A and B concern notice and frequency, not what the test proves, so neither closes the gap against the top-rated scenario.
Final two: D beats C because no test assumes the online backups are lost, the condition behind the bank's highest risk; a wider scope without that condition proves no more.
Exam cue: judge a recovery test by the risk scenarios it exercises; the GREATEST concern is usually a top-rated scenario left untested.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5 (Plan Testing, Training, and Exercises); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Indicator for a backup control
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST key control indicator for a magazine publisher's backup control?

options.A: Share of test restores that meet the RTO and RPO targets
options.B: Share of scheduled backup jobs that finish without error
options.C: Number of ransomware incidents in the past year
options.D: Backup storage used as a share of capacity

questions.key_concept: A KCI shows whether a control achieves its purpose; for backups, that is test restores within RTO and RPO, not completed backup jobs.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the backup control exists to achieve before judging each measure.
questions.correct_explanation: A key control indicator shows whether a control is working well enough to keep risk in check. A backup control exists so data can be recovered within the business's recovery objectives, and only test restores measured against the RTO and RPO show that. Backup job success is the runner-up: it shows copies were written, but not that they can be restored, are complete or are fast enough.

wrong_explanations.B: Job success is worth tracking as a process measure; however, a job can finish cleanly and still produce copies that cannot be restored in time.
wrong_explanations.C: Incident counts show outcomes after the fact; however, they say little about whether backups work, and a quiet year proves nothing about recovery.
wrong_explanations.D: Storage use is an operational capacity measure; however, it shows nothing about whether the backups can actually be restored.

tips: Eliminate: C counts past incidents instead of measuring the control, and D tracks storage capacity, an operations measure.
Final two: A beats B because a backup control exists for recovery; restores tested against RTO and RPO show it works, while finished jobs only show copies exist.
Exam cue: a KCI measures whether a control achieves its purpose; pick the measure of the outcome the control exists for, not of its activity.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Pilot with little loss data
questions.question: A distributor's leaders approved a six-month pilot of augmented-reality headsets for warehouse picking, though little data exists on how they fail. What is MOST important for the risk practitioner to have agreed before it starts?

options.A: Loss data from other firms that use the headsets
options.B: Pilot controls matching those on live picking systems
options.C: Conditions under which the pilot would be paused
options.D: Vendor certification of the headsets' security

questions.key_concept: With little data on an emerging technology, run the pilot under pause conditions agreed from appetite with the business owner, limiting loss as evidence builds.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much is known about the headsets and what that means for planning their controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Little data means nobody yet knows how the headsets will fail in live picking, so controls cannot be sized with confidence. Agreeing in advance what would pause the pilot, such as error rates, injuries or data issues set from appetite with the warehouse owner, limits loss whatever happens while the pilot builds evidence to rate the risk. Copying the live systems' controls is the runner-up: it covers only failures someone has foreseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Other firms' losses add context; however, their sites and uses differ, and for a new technology that data is thin, so it cannot bound this pilot's risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Some controls will be needed; however, copying the live systems' controls assumes failure modes nobody yet knows and does not limit loss if the headsets fail in a new way.
wrong_explanations.D: Certification is useful evidence; however, it covers the product's security within a scope, not how the headsets fail in this warehouse's picking work.

tips: Eliminate: A borrows thin data from other sites, and D covers the product's security, not how the headsets fail in this warehouse.
Final two: C beats B because, with failure modes unknown, agreed pause conditions limit loss whatever happens; copied controls cover only failures someone has foreseen.
Exam cue: when an emerging technology has little data, pilot it under agreed limits and stop conditions set from appetite, and let the evidence firm up the rating.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Exit terms for a young vendor
questions.question: A logistics firm's evaluation of a start-up's drone delivery platform weighs benefits and threats; the platform would hold all route data in its own format. What is the GREATEST gap the risk practitioner should raise?

options.A: No exit terms if the vendor fails or is sold
options.B: No dollar value for each threat it lists
options.C: No check of the vendor's certifications
options.D: No pilot of the platform before the evaluation

questions.key_concept: Emerging technology from a young vendor needs exit terms, such as data return in a usable format; lock-in makes the vendor's failure the enterprise's outage.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the evaluation already covers and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: The evaluation weighs benefits and threats, but the deciding facts are a start-up vendor and route data held in its own format. If the vendor fails or is sold, the firm could lose the data and the service, so exit terms such as data return in a usable format and a transition period are the largest gap. Missing certifications are the runner-up: they matter for security, but they say nothing about surviving the vendor's failure.

wrong_explanations.B: Dollar values can sharpen the evaluation; however, a qualitative view is acceptable at this stage, and pricing threats does not address the lock-in.
wrong_explanations.C: Certifications describe the vendor's controls today; however, they do not protect the firm if the start-up fails or the data cannot leave its format.
wrong_explanations.D: Evaluating before a pilot is normal and helps set the pilot's conditions; it is not a gap in the evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: B prices threats without touching the lock-in, and D treats evaluating before a pilot as a flaw.
Final two: A beats C because the stem's risk is dependence on a young vendor's format; certifications show controls today, not a way out.
Exam cue: when a new technology locks data into one vendor, look for exit terms and data return before adoption.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Value of a framework mapping
questions.question: Which of the following is the PRIMARY value to a risk practitioner of mapping an organization's security practices to NIST CSF 2.0?

options.A: Certification that the controls meet the framework
options.B: Proof that residual risk sits within appetite
options.C: A ready-made control list for the firm to adopt
options.D: A common way to compare current and target outcomes

questions.key_concept: A framework mapping gives a common language for current and target outcomes; risk and cost-benefit, not the framework, decide what to close.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework is designed to give an organization, and what it is not.
questions.correct_explanation: CSF 2.0 describes outcomes, not a control checklist, and its Profiles describe the outcomes an organization achieves now and those it selects as targets. Mapping practices to those outcomes gives the practitioner a common way to show the gap between current and target, which owners can then prioritize by risk. A ready-made control list is the runner-up: the framework is tailored, so the mapping informs choices rather than dictating them.

wrong_explanations.A: Alignment can be shown to others; however, CSF 2.0 is a voluntary outcomes framework, and a mapping shows alignment, not a certified status.
wrong_explanations.B: A mapping shows which outcomes are achieved; however, whether residual risk is within appetite needs the scenarios themselves rated on evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: The mapping does show outcomes with no practice behind them; however, CSF outcomes are tailored to the organization's risks and do not form a mandatory control list.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a voluntary framework as something that certifies, and B treats alignment with outcomes as proof that risk is within appetite.
Final two: D beats C because CSF outcomes are tailored to risk; the mapping shows current against target, not a fixed list of controls to adopt.
Exam cue: a framework gives a common language and a gap view; risk and cost-benefit decide what to close, and a framework result is never a risk rating.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Length of elevated access
questions.question: A payroll software provider grants developers production administrator access on request for 30 days at a time, though each emergency fix takes about four hours. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Remove developers' administrator access to production
options.B: Limit each grant to the task and a few hours
options.C: Review each developer's administrator grants periodically
options.D: Record each developer's acceptance of the access risk

questions.key_concept: Least privilege applies to time as well as scope: size each grant of elevated access to the task, not to a convenient period.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each grant allows and how the work it serves is done.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege covers time as well as scope. A 30-day grant for a fix that takes four hours leaves production administrator rights open far longer than the work needs, for an attacker or a mistake to use. Limiting each grant to the task and a few hours keeps emergency fixes possible while removing most of that exposure. Removing access is the runner-up: it cuts the risk but leaves no fast route for real emergencies.

wrong_explanations.A: Removal cuts exposure most and fits separation of duties; however, it leaves no fast way to fix production in a real emergency, trading one risk for another.
wrong_explanations.C: Periodic review is useful; however, it does nothing about 30-day grants that outlast each task.
wrong_explanations.D: Signed acknowledgments raise awareness; however, individual developers cannot accept organizational risk, and the long grants stay in place.

tips: Eliminate: C reviews grants periodically without shortening any of them, and D asks individuals to accept a risk that belongs to the risk owner.
Final two: B beats A because a grant sized to the task meets the emergency need with least privilege; removal cuts exposure but disables emergency response.
Exam cue: least privilege applies to time as well as scope; size each grant of elevated access to the task, not to a convenient period.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Partial Zero Trust rollout
questions.question: A shipping line bought a Zero Trust access product, and its IT director reports that 20% of remote users now connect through it. What is the BEST basis for the risk practitioner's remote-access risk rating?

options.A: Target risk once the rollout is complete
options.B: Inherent risk until the users finish moving
options.C: Current risk, crediting users already moved
options.D: Risk accepted on record until the rollout ends

questions.key_concept: Current risk credits only controls in place and working; a partly deployed Zero Trust product reduces risk only where it is live.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has been bought and what is actually in use today.
questions.correct_explanation: A register rating records current risk, which counts controls already in place and working, not ones bought or planned. With 80% of remote users still on the old path, most remote access has no Zero Trust protection yet, so the rating should credit only the coverage that is live. Target risk once the rollout is complete is the runner-up: it judges whether the plan is enough, not today's position.

wrong_explanations.A: Target risk shows where the plan should lead; however, it credits protection 80% of remote users do not yet have, so it overstates today's exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Inherent risk avoids overstating the protection; however, it ignores the controls that do work, including the 20% of users already moved.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners may accept residual risk within appetite; however, acceptance is a response made on an accurate rating, not a basis for the rating itself.

tips: Eliminate: B sets aside the coverage already live, and D treats the owner's acceptance as the basis for a rating that acceptance should follow.
Final two: C beats A because current risk counts only controls in place and working; target risk judges whether the rollout plan is enough, not today's position.
Exam cue: a purchase or a plan is not a working control; rate current risk on what is live, and treat the plan's outcome as target risk.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Accountability for risk culture
questions.question: A software firm's CEO wants the risk practitioner to be accountable for improving the firm's risk culture. What is the practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Accept the accountability and report progress to the board
options.B: Propose that HR take the accountability within training
options.C: Propose that internal audit take the accountability
options.D: Propose that the executive team keep the accountability

questions.key_concept: Executive leadership is accountable for risk culture; the risk practitioner promotes, measures and reports on it, and internal audit assures it independently.
questions.pre_read: Ask who shapes culture through tone, rewards and priorities, and who supports them.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk culture follows what leaders say, reward and do, so accountability for it sits with executive leadership; NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 makes leadership accountable for fostering a risk-aware culture. The practitioner still promotes that culture by designing measures, running surveys and reporting results. Accepting the accountability is the runner-up: it is helpful in spirit, but places culture with a support function that cannot set the firm's tone, incentives or priorities.

wrong_explanations.A: The practitioner can run culture surveys and reporting; however, accountability for culture stays with the leaders whose tone and incentives shape it, which a risk function cannot set.
wrong_explanations.B: HR can deliver training and adjust incentives; however, culture goes beyond training, and accountability for it belongs to the executive team that sets the tone.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit can assess culture independently; however, taking accountability for it would compromise the independence it needs to give assurance.

tips: Eliminate: B narrows culture to training, and C gives accountability to internal audit, whose role is independent assurance.
Final two: D beats A because leaders are accountable for the culture they shape; the practitioner measures and supports it without holding that accountability.
Exam cue: tone at the top means leadership owns risk culture; the risk function promotes, measures and reports, and internal audit gives assurance.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Error blamed on one clerk
questions.question: A builders' merchant's accounts clerk paid a fake invoice while following the documented payment process to the letter. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A verification step in the payment process
options.B: Removal of the clerk from the payment process
options.C: Retraining for the finance team on fake invoices
options.D: Targeted fraud awareness tests for the clerk

questions.key_concept: When an error follows the documented process, the process is the root cause; fix it before blaming or retraining the person.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the clerk broke the process or followed it.
questions.correct_explanation: The clerk did what the documented process asked, so the failure lies in a process that lets a convincing invoice be paid without an independent check. Adding a verification step, such as confirming payment details with the supplier through known contacts, removes that cause. Retraining the team is the runner-up: it helps staff spot fakes, but a well-made fake can still pass while the process gap stays open.

wrong_explanations.B: Accountability matters for willful misconduct; however, this clerk followed the process, and removing them would leave the gap open and teach staff to hide mistakes.
wrong_explanations.C: Training helps staff spot fakes; however, it relies on people catching every well-made invoice while the process still has no independent check.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra tests could raise one person's awareness; however, singling out the clerk treats a process gap as a personal failing and leaves it open.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes a clerk who followed the process, and D targets one person's awareness while the process gap stays open.
Final two: A beats C because the process let the fake through; a verification step removes the cause, while training depends on spotting every fake.
Exam cue: when someone errs while following the process, fix the process first; discipline is for willful or repeated misconduct, and blame suppresses reporting.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Evidence of privacy by design
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a risk practitioner that a bank's new budgeting app was built with privacy by design?

options.A: Encryption of customers' personal data at rest and in transit
options.B: Default settings that collect only what each feature needs
options.C: A privacy notice that lists each use of the customers' data
options.D: A privacy impact assessment completed after the launch

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design shows in the system itself, especially protective defaults that collect only what each feature needs.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option is part of how the app was built rather than added around it.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy by design means privacy is built into the engineering, and its clearest sign is protective defaults: the app collects only what each feature needs unless the customer chooses more. A privacy notice is the runner-up: transparency is a real privacy principle, but a notice can accurately describe heavy collection, so it shows disclosure, not design.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects data from unauthorized access; however, it is a security control and says nothing about how much data the app collects or why.
wrong_explanations.C: Telling customers about each use supports transparency; however, a notice can accurately describe excessive collection, so it shows disclosure rather than design.
wrong_explanations.D: A privacy impact assessment is valuable; however, done after launch it documents choices already made instead of shaping the design.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security control, not a privacy design choice, and D assesses privacy only after the design is fixed.
Final two: B beats C because protective defaults are built into the app itself; a notice discloses what happens without limiting it.
Exam cue: privacy by design shows in the system's defaults and minimal collection; encryption, notices and late assessments show other things.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Releasing de-identified trip data
questions.question: A transit authority's data team will publish trip records that give each card one fixed random code and keep exact times and stops. What is the GREATEST privacy risk the risk practitioner should raise?

options.A: Decrypting the codes back into the card numbers
options.B: Errors in the trip data that mislead outside researchers
options.C: Linking each code's travel pattern to a known person
options.D: Authority staff misusing the records once published

questions.key_concept: De-identified records can be re-identified by linking what remains, such as exact times and places, to known people.
questions.pre_read: Look at what the authority keeps in the records, not only what it removes.
questions.correct_explanation: Replacing card numbers does not make data anonymous when each code follows one person and exact times and stops remain. A few known trips, such as a home stop at a regular hour, can tie a code to a person and expose all their travel. Decrypting the codes is the runner-up: random replacement values have no key to break, so the real exposure is linkage, not decryption.

wrong_explanations.A: Weak pseudonyms can sometimes be reversed; however, these codes are random replacements, not encrypted card numbers, so there is nothing to decrypt.
wrong_explanations.B: Data quality matters for research; however, errors mislead users of the data, while the privacy question is whether people can be identified.
wrong_explanations.D: Insider misuse is a real concern; however, once published the records are open to everyone, so staff access adds little to the exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B is a data quality concern, not a privacy one, and D worries about insiders when the data will be public.
Final two: C beats A because random codes cannot be decrypted, but a stable code with exact times and stops can be linked to a person.
Exam cue: de-identified data can still be re-identified; look at what remains, such as exact times, places or rare details, not just what was removed.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Moving records to another country
questions.question: An engineering firm's HR director wants to move employee records to a cloud provider's data center in another country next month. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the employee records before they are moved
options.B: Rely on the provider's statement that the region is compliant
options.C: Tell employees about the move once it is complete
options.D: Ask legal counsel to confirm the transfer is permitted

questions.key_concept: Personal data keeps its legal protection across borders; confirm with legal counsel that a transfer is permitted before the data moves.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of data is moving and where, then ask what must be settled before it moves.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving personal data across borders can be restricted by the law that protects it, and this move is a month away. Whether it is permitted, and on what conditions, is settled before the data moves, with legal counsel advising and the data owner deciding. Encryption is the runner-up: it protects the records in transit and storage, but it does not make an unlawful transfer lawful.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption is a sound safeguard; however, it is a security control, and it does not settle whether the law allows the records to be moved.
wrong_explanations.B: Provider assurances help; however, the firm stays accountable for its employees' data, and a sales statement is not legal confirmation for this transfer.
wrong_explanations.C: Telling employees supports transparency; however, notice after the move comes too late if the transfer needed a legal basis or prior notice.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the provider's claim for a duty that stays with the firm, and C informs employees only after the move is done.
Final two: D beats A because a transfer must be lawful before it happens; encryption protects the data but does not make the move permitted.
Exam cue: for cross-border transfers, confirm the legal basis FIRST with counsel; security controls follow, never in place of it.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Judging an integration's impact
questions.question: Which of the following BEST helps a risk practitioner judge the business impact of connecting a new claims platform to an insurer's existing systems?

options.A: The vendor's security architecture document for the platform
options.B: The network diagram of the platform's planned connections
options.C: The enterprise architecture's links among processes and data
options.D: The project's integration test plan for the new platform

questions.key_concept: Enterprise architecture links business processes, data, applications and technology, so it shows what a change touches and its business impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the practitioner must judge, then ask which source connects technology to the business.
questions.correct_explanation: Business impact depends on which processes and data the new platform would touch, and the enterprise architecture is the model that links business processes, data, applications and technology. The network diagram is the runner-up: it shows the planned technical connections, but not which claims processes or data sets would suffer if a connection failed or was breached.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's architecture document describes the product's own design; it does not show which of the insurer's processes and data the connection would touch.
wrong_explanations.B: A network diagram shows how systems connect at the technical layer; it does not show which business processes and data depend on those connections.
wrong_explanations.D: An integration test plan checks that the connections work before go-live; it does not show what the business would lose if they failed.

tips: Eliminate: A describes only the vendor's product, and D checks that the build works; neither maps the insurer's processes and data.
Final two: C beats B because business impact needs the link from systems to processes and data; a network diagram stops at the technical layer.
Exam cue: when an item asks for the business impact of a technology change, choose the source that ties technology to business processes.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Extracts sent to a research partner
questions.question: An electricity distributor's data owner signed an agreement letting a university partner study household energy use, and the monthly smart-meter extracts include customers' names and street addresses. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the extracts before each email is sent
options.B: Add a confidentiality clause to the sharing agreement
options.C: Stop the sharing until the partner passes a security audit
options.D: Remove the identifiers the agreed research does not need

questions.key_concept: At the sharing stage, send only what the agreed purpose needs; clauses and encryption do not reduce the exposure of data that need not leave.
questions.pre_read: Compare the purpose the owner approved with what each extract contains.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner has set the purpose, a study of household energy use, and names and street addresses are not needed for it. Removing the identifiers the study does not need, before each extract leaves, cuts the exposure at its source: data never sent cannot be misused or breached at the partner. A confidentiality clause is the runner-up: it limits what the partner may do, but full identities would still leave the distributor every month.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects the extracts in transit only; once the partner opens them, every name and address is still there.
wrong_explanations.B: A clause binds the partner's use, but the distributor still sends identities the study does not need, so a breach or misuse at the partner exposes them.
wrong_explanations.C: An audit checks the partner's safeguards but does not reduce the personal data sent, and halting a sharing the owner approved is not the practitioner's call.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the email but not the data at the partner, and C audits the partner while the excess data keeps flowing.
Final two: D beats B because data that is never sent cannot be misused; a clause limits use but still ships every identity.
Exam cue: when data is shared for an agreed purpose, the strongest control is not sending what that purpose does not need; clauses and audits govern only what is sent.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. AI agent acting on its own
questions.question: A manufacturer plans to let an AI maintenance agent order spare parts and schedule line shutdowns on its own. What is MOST important for the risk practitioner to have agreed before go-live?

options.A: A contract making the vendor liable for wrong orders
options.B: Limits on what the agent may do without approval
options.C: The vendor's certification of its model's security
options.D: A KRI tracking the value of parts the agent orders

questions.key_concept: An AI agent that acts on its own needs limits on what it may do without human approval, set by the impact of its actions.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the agent will do, not only what it will predict.
questions.correct_explanation: Ordering parts and stopping production lines are business decisions with real cost; an agent that takes them unaided turns any wrong prediction into an immediate loss. Limits agreed first, such as spending caps and human approval before any line shutdown, sized to each action's impact, keep the agent within appetite. A KRI on parts ordered is the runner-up: it shows problems, but only after the agent has acted.

wrong_explanations.A: A liability clause shifts some of the cost of a wrong order, not the lost production or the plant's accountability for what the agent does.
wrong_explanations.C: A security certificate speaks to the vendor's controls, not to what the agent is allowed to do in the plant.
wrong_explanations.D: A KRI warns when ordering climbs, but only after orders and shutdowns have happened; it does not stop a costly action before it is taken.

tips: Eliminate: A shifts some cost to the vendor but not the lost production, and C answers a security question rather than what the agent may do.
Final two: B beats D because limits stop a costly action before it happens; a KRI warns only after the agent has acted.
Exam cue: when AI can act, not just advise, size what it may do alone to the impact of each action; contracts and indicators come second.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Executives exempt from a control
questions.question: In a property developer's staff survey, most respondents say security rules feel optional because senior executives were exempted from the new sign-in checks. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A refresher security course for the whole staff
options.B: Disciplinary action for staff who bypass the sign-in checks
options.C: Executives using the same sign-in checks as their staff
options.D: A message from the CEO on why security rules matter

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top is set by leaders' actions; leaders exempt from a control signal that the control does not matter.
questions.pre_read: Notice why staff say the rules feel optional, then ask which option removes that reason.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff are reading the exemption as the real message: if leaders skip a control, the control must not matter. Culture follows what leaders do, so the fix is for executives to use the same checks. A message from the CEO is the runner-up; it sets the right words, but while the exemption stands, staff will believe the behavior rather than the message.

wrong_explanations.A: Staff already know the rules; the survey says they doubt them because of the exemption, which more training does not change.
wrong_explanations.B: Punishing staff treats a culture signal as misconduct and leaves in place the exemption that caused the doubt.
wrong_explanations.D: A CEO message answers a signal that was sent in words; here the signal is an exemption, and staff will weigh any message against what the executives visibly do.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains staff who already know the rules, and B punishes staff for a doubt that leaders created.
Final two: C beats D because tone at the top is set by what leaders do; a message cannot outweigh a visible exemption.
Exam cue: when a culture problem traces to leaders' own behavior, the BEST fix changes that behavior rather than training staff.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Approving pipeline releases
questions.question: To show tighter control, a fintech's CTO proposes that the risk analyst approve every production release in the CI/CD pipeline, which already enforces peer review and automated tests. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Accept the role and approve each release within agreed hours
options.B: Monitor the release gates that engineering runs
options.C: Refer each release to internal audit for approval
options.D: Have the change board approve each production release

questions.key_concept: In DevOps, engineering owns release controls in the pipeline; the risk function monitors and challenges them rather than approving releases.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is asked to approve releases, then ask which line of defense should run that control.
questions.correct_explanation: Release approval is a first-line control: engineering runs it through the pipeline's peer review and tests, and the engineering lead is accountable for it working. The analyst, in the second line, monitors whether the gates work and reports exceptions. Taking the approval is the runner-up; it looks like tighter control, but the analyst would then operate a control they are meant to challenge.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving releases makes the second line operate a first-line control, so the analyst would later be checking their own work.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; approving releases would make it part of the control it later audits.
wrong_explanations.D: A change board vote on each release repeats checks the pipeline already enforces, adding delay without improving oversight of the gates.

tips: Eliminate: C puts the third line inside a control it audits, and D adds a manual vote on top of gates that already enforce review.
Final two: B beats A because the second line monitors and challenges first-line controls; approving releases would make it operate one.
Exam cue: when asked to run or approve an operational control, the practitioner leaves it with the first line and monitors it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Delay in a shared dependency
questions.question: A regional bank's network upgrade has slipped nine months, yet three projects that need it before launch still report green status to the portfolio board. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Ask the network project to recover its original date
options.B: Update the three projects' status with their managers
options.C: Pause the three dependent projects until the upgrade ends
options.D: Analyze the three projects' combined risk with the delay

questions.key_concept: Project dependencies carry risk across a portfolio; a delay is reassessed in every dependent project so the portfolio board decides on a true picture.
questions.pre_read: Notice what links the four projects, then ask what the board's green status is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: One project's delay pushes risk into every project that depends on it, and green status shows the board has not seen it. Analyzing the three projects' risk together, with the slip included, gives the portfolio board one true picture to decide on. Pausing them is the runner-up; it may prove the right outcome, but it is the board's decision, made after the risk is analyzed.

wrong_explanations.A: Pressing for the original date targets the schedule, not the exposure; a rushed upgrade can add risk, and the dependent projects stay misreported.
wrong_explanations.B: Updating status with the managers acts before analysis; until the combined dependency risk is known, no one can say what the true status is.
wrong_explanations.C: Pausing may be justified; however, it is the portfolio board's call, and making it before the risk is analyzed skips that decision.

tips: Eliminate: A chases the date instead of the exposure, and B asks for the same self-reported status that already shows green.
Final two: D beats C because the board needs the analyzed risk before choosing to pause; pausing first decides for it.
Exam cue: when one project's delay affects others, look across the portfolio and analyze before anyone changes the plan.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A5.1 (Portfolio Management by Value and Risk: the portfolio is reviewed as value and risk change, and dependencies are tracked because one delay can push risk into others). questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Same flaw in every release
questions.question: In four releases running, penetration tests of a car rental firm's booking portal have found the same kind of injection flaw, fixed each time before launch. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A penetration test before each minor release as well
options.B: A web application firewall in front of the booking portal
options.C: A review of how the flaw keeps getting into the code
options.D: A faster fix process that closes each flaw within a day

questions.key_concept: Recurring vulnerabilities of one kind point to a gap in the development process; root cause analysis changes the process so the flaw stops recurring.
questions.pre_read: Notice how often the flaw appears, then ask what that pattern says about where it comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: A flaw that returns in four releases points to a gap in how the code is written, such as a secure coding practice that is not followed or not taught. Analyzing that root cause lets the development process change so the flaw stops entering the code. A web application firewall is the runner-up; it can reduce exposure, but the same flaws keep being written behind it.

wrong_explanations.A: More testing finds the flaw more often; it does not stop developers writing it, so the find-and-fix cycle continues each release.
wrong_explanations.B: A firewall can block some attacks as a compensating layer; however, the code keeps producing the same flaw, which the process should stop.
wrong_explanations.D: Faster fixes shorten each exposure but treat every finding as new, leaving the cause of the repeats in place.

tips: Eliminate: A and D speed up finding and fixing each flaw, so both treat symptoms while the same flaw keeps being written.
Final two: C beats B because a repeat flaw signals a process gap; a firewall shields the portal but leaves the cause.
Exam cue: when the same finding recurs, the BEST recommendation targets its root cause in the process that produces it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 RV.3 (Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes: analyze root causes over time and update the SDLC process so they do not recur)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A3.2 (Secure Development and Testing: testing finds flaws while a secure development process prevents them, and a flaw that recurs across releases signals a process gap). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (car rental firm's booking portal with the same injection flaw four releases running) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used; checked against the CRISC, CISA, CC and AAIA banks for mirrored scenarios. questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Removing layers around customer data
questions.question: A retailer's IT director proposes dropping database encryption and activity monitoring for customer records, since a recent test found the network segmentation around them strong. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Reliance on a single test of the segmentation's strength
options.B: Higher cost of adding the controls back at a later date
options.C: Customer records left behind one control with no detection
options.D: Loss of the audit trail on customer records for investigations

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth keeps several independent controls on critical assets, so one failure does not expose them unseen.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many controls would remain around the records, then ask what happens if that one fails.
questions.correct_explanation: Defense in depth means an attacker must defeat several controls, and each layer can catch what another misses. Without encryption and monitoring, any segmentation failure, such as a misconfigured rule or a stolen administrator login, would expose customer records with nothing to stop or reveal it. Reliance on one test is the runner-up; it weakens the evidence, but even proven segmentation stays a single layer.

wrong_explanations.A: One test is thin evidence of lasting strength; however, even segmentation tested every week would still leave the records behind a single layer.
wrong_explanations.B: The cost of reinstating controls is a budget question; the larger issue is the exposure while only one control stands.
wrong_explanations.D: Losing activity logs hampers later investigations; the greater concern is that a breach would be neither stopped nor noticed while it happens.

tips: Eliminate: B weighs a future budget cost, and D looks at investigations after the fact instead of the exposure itself.
Final two: C beats A because no single control is enough for critical data; even proven segmentation can fail.
Exam cue: when a proposal removes layers because one control tests strong, the GREATEST concern is the single point of failure left behind.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B1.1 (Core Security Principles: no single control is enough for a critical asset, so layered, independent controls mean one failure does not expose it). questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Strategy change and an old roadmap
questions.question: A furniture retailer's board approved a strategy to make online sales half of revenue in three years, but the technology roadmap is unchanged since 2024. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: IT investments that no longer serve the strategy
options.B: Rising technical debt in the systems the roadmap retains
options.C: Vendor contracts renewing before the roadmap is revised
options.D: Higher costs when the strategy's online systems come late

questions.key_concept: A technology roadmap serves business strategy; when strategy changes, an unchanged roadmap puts the new objectives at risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed and what did not, then ask what the roadmap is for.
questions.correct_explanation: A roadmap exists to schedule technology change in support of business objectives. When the strategy moves to online sales and the roadmap does not, money and effort keep flowing to plans made for the old goals, and the systems the new strategy needs may arrive late or not at all. Rising technical debt is the runner-up; it may grow, but it is one effect of the larger misalignment.

wrong_explanations.B: Technical debt may build in the systems the roadmap keeps; it is a narrower effect of a roadmap that no longer matches the strategy.
wrong_explanations.C: Renewals may lock in old choices; that is one narrow effect of the stale roadmap, and the stem gives no renewal dates to weigh.
wrong_explanations.D: Late additions may cost more; that is a consequence of the misalignment rather than the risk to the strategy itself.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are narrow cost effects of the stale roadmap, not the risk to what the board wants to achieve.
Final two: A beats B because the roadmap's job is to serve strategy; misalignment threatens the objective, while debt is one symptom.
Exam cue: when strategy changes and the plans beneath it do not, the GREATEST risk is to the new business objectives.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A1.2 (Technology Roadmaps and Off-Roadmap Technology: the roadmap links each technology change to a business objective and is reviewed when strategy changes). questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Apps built on a low-code platform
questions.question: Operations staff at an insurer have built 40 workflow apps on a newly licensed low-code platform, and some move claims payment data. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Have the platform owner suspend it until apps are rebuilt
options.B: Rely on the platform vendor's security certification
options.C: Inventory the apps with their owners and the data they use
options.D: Assess the platform's security settings with the vendor

questions.key_concept: Apps that business staff build on emerging platforms are inventoried with owners and data before their risk can be assessed.
questions.pre_read: Notice what staff have built and what data it moves, then ask what the practitioner needs to know first.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk sits in what staff have built: 40 apps, some moving payment data, with no record yet of who owns each one. An inventory naming each app's owner and data is what any assessment starts from. Reviewing the platform's settings with the vendor is the runner-up; it matters, but it shows nothing about which apps handle payments or who is accountable for them.

wrong_explanations.A: Suspending the platform halts useful work before the risk is known, and pushes staff toward spreadsheets and other unmanaged tools.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor certificate covers the vendor's platform, not the apps staff built on it or the payment data those apps move.
wrong_explanations.D: Platform settings matter; however, without knowing which apps exist and what data each uses, the review cannot tell where the risk is.

tips: Eliminate: A halts the platform before any risk is known, and B relies on a vendor certificate that does not cover staff-built apps.
Final two: C beats D because the risk sits in the apps and their data; the inventory comes before any platform review.
Exam cue: when business users adopt a new technology widely, FIRST find what exists, who owns it and what data it touches.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Disruption from a full test
questions.question: A frozen-food wholesaler's recovery plan passed tabletop and parallel tests last year; the IT director now plans a full interruption test that would halt deliveries if recovery fails. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Have the plan owner, the IT director, set the test date
options.B: Repeat last year's parallel test in place of the full test
options.C: Take the disruption risk of a failed test to the business owner
options.D: Ask internal audit to approve the test for the business

questions.key_concept: The business owner decides how much test disruption to accept; the practitioner shows what a failed test could cost the process.
questions.pre_read: Notice how far the plan has been tested, then ask who bears the cost if this test fails.
questions.correct_explanation: Having passed tabletop and parallel tests, the plan is ready for a more realistic test, but a failed full interruption test would halt deliveries. That business impact is for the business owner of the delivery operation to accept or limit, for example through timing and a fallback. Repeating the parallel test is the runner-up; it lowers disruption, but it makes the owner's call for them and leaves full recovery unproven.

wrong_explanations.A: The IT director owns the plan, not the deliveries a failed test could halt; that disruption is the business owner's to accept.
wrong_explanations.B: A repeat parallel test lowers disruption; however, the plan has already passed one, and choosing the lighter test makes the owner's decision for them.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives assurance on testing; approving the test would put it inside a decision that belongs to the business owner.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves a business disruption decision with IT, and D puts internal audit in charge of a test it may later review.
Final two: C beats B because the owner decides how much test disruption to accept; swapping in a lighter test makes that call for them.
Exam cue: when a recovery test could disrupt the business, the business owner accepts or limits that disruption, informed by the practitioner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing); ISACA Glossary (risk owner)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A6.3 (Testing Recovery Capability: tests are chosen by risk and plan maturity, and the business owner decides how much test disruption to accept). questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Use after a block on AI sites
questions.question: After an accounting firm blocked public AI chat sites on its network, a staff survey shows many now paste client figures into them from personal phones. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Extend the block to personal phones on the guest Wi-Fi
options.B: Discipline staff who admit using personal phones for work
options.C: Add the AI chat risk to the staff awareness course
options.D: Offer an approved AI tool with clear rules on client data

questions.key_concept: Shadow AI is reduced by pairing clear guidance with an approved tool; bans without an alternative push use out of sight.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happened after the block, then ask why staff keep using the tools.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff still need what the tools give them, so the block moved the use onto devices the firm cannot see. An approved tool with clear rules on client data meets that need inside controls the firm can monitor. Awareness training is the runner-up; staff should know the rules, but guidance without an approved alternative leaves them choosing between the rule and the work.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking more networks pushes use further out of sight, because phones on mobile data bypass any Wi-Fi block.
wrong_explanations.B: Punishing staff who admit the habit discourages honest answers and leaves unmet the need that drives the use.
wrong_explanations.C: Awareness is part of the answer; however, a course without an approved tool leaves staff with the same need and the same workaround.

tips: Eliminate: A pushes use further out of sight, and B discourages the honest reporting the survey depended on.
Final two: D beats C because guidance works when paired with an approved alternative; training alone leaves the need unmet.
Exam cue: when a ban drives use underground, the BEST answer meets the business need through an approved, controlled option.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind); ISACA Glossary (shadow IT)

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Training copies with no end date
questions.question: A telecom's retention schedule deletes customer chat logs after one year, but its data science team keeps full copies in a model training set with no end date. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data owner rule on keeping the training copies longer
options.B: Lock the training copies to named data scientists' accounts
options.C: Delete the trained models along with the log copies
options.D: Make the data science team owner of the training copies

questions.key_concept: AI training sets are copies of business data, so the source's retention schedule covers them, and only the data owner can approve keeping them longer.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the copies sit and who decided how long to keep them.
questions.correct_explanation: Training copies are still customer chat logs, so the one-year schedule covers them. Keeping them longer for training is a new use only the data owner, with legal advice, can approve; until the owner rules, the copies are due for deletion like any data past its period. Restricting access is the runner-up: it lowers misuse risk, but the copies would still be kept past the schedule with no one accountable approving it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tighter access lowers misuse risk; however, the copies are still kept with no end date the data owner has approved, past the one-year schedule for the source logs.
wrong_explanations.C: Deleting the models goes beyond the problem; the owner may allow training for a set period, and models can be retrained if needed.
wrong_explanations.D: The data science team uses the copies; ownership of customer data stays with the business manager accountable for it.

tips: Eliminate: C destroys models before the owner has decided anything, and D hands ownership to the team that uses the data.
Final two: A beats B because keeping data past the schedule is the data owner's decision; tighter access still leaves the copies kept with no end date.
Exam cue: copies made for AI training fall under the source data's owner and schedule; a new business need to keep data longer goes to the owner, and data nobody needs is deleted on schedule.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). A change called too small to review
questions.question: A developer at a staffing agency says a new button that exports full payroll records to spreadsheets is too small a change to need risk review. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Treat the export as a pre-approved standard change
options.B: Assess what the export exposes before it is approved
options.C: Assess the export button once it is in production
options.D: Ask the payroll owner to sign acceptance of the export's risk

questions.key_concept: Change risk depends on the data and processes a change touches, not its size; impact is assessed before approval.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the button would let users do, then ask whether its size decides its risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The size of the code change says little about risk: one button would let anyone with access take full payroll records out of the system. The change's impact is analyzed before approval, so the owner and change authority decide on the facts. Asking the payroll owner to accept the risk is the runner-up; the owner does decide, but acceptance before analysis is acceptance of an unknown.

wrong_explanations.A: Pre-approval suits low-risk, repeatable changes; an export of full payroll records has not been shown to be low risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Assessing in production finds the exposure after payroll data may already have left the system.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner does accept change risk; however, asking before the exposure is analyzed asks them to accept something no one has measured.

tips: Eliminate: A pre-approves a change no one has shown to be low risk, and C looks at the risk only after release.
Final two: B beats D because acceptance follows analysis; the owner cannot accept an exposure that has not been assessed.
Exam cue: judge a change by the data and process it touches, not by how much code it takes.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Deletion requests that miss copies
questions.question: Sampling 20 of a meal-kit company's completed deletion requests, the risk analyst finds every customer's details still held in its analytics warehouse and email marketing tool. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Delete the sampled customers' details from both systems
options.B: Encrypt the customer details held in both systems
options.C: Test a larger sample of deletion requests before reporting
options.D: Add each customer data store to the deletion process

questions.key_concept: Individual rights requests can be met only when the organization knows every system holding the person's data.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many sampled requests failed and where, then ask what that pattern points to.
questions.correct_explanation: Every sampled request missed the same two systems, so the deletion process reaches only part of where customer data lives. Bringing each system that holds customer data into the process makes every request reach every copy, and past requests can then be run through it again. Deleting the sampled customers' details is the runner-up; it fixes those 20 cases, but the process would keep missing the same two systems for every other request.

wrong_explanations.A: Clearing the sampled records fixes 20 cases; the process would still miss the same two systems for every other request.
wrong_explanations.B: Encryption protects the copies from outsiders; it does not meet the customers' requests to have their data deleted.
wrong_explanations.C: A larger sample adds little when all 20 failed the same way; the pattern already shows a process gap to fix.

tips: Eliminate: B protects data customers asked to have deleted, and C delays a finding that 20 failures out of 20 already prove.
Final two: D beats A because every sampled request failed the same way; fixing the process reaches all requests, not just the sample.
Exam cue: when a sample shows the same failure in every case, the BEST recommendation fixes the process that produced it.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Indicator for an Agile program
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST key risk indicator of security risk building up in a bank's Agile delivery program?

options.A: Number of sprints the teams complete on schedule
options.B: Count of security backlog items deferred across sprints
options.C: Number of security flaws found in production
options.D: Share of team members who finished secure coding training

questions.key_concept: A leading KRI for Agile delivery tracks deferred security work across sprints, warning before flaws reach production.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words building up, then ask what each measure would show and when.
questions.correct_explanation: A key risk indicator should warn before the loss, and deferred security work is risk the program is choosing to carry into later releases. A rising count across sprints signals exposure building before it reaches customers. Flaws found in production are the runner-up; they are relevant, but they count damage already shipped, so they report the risk after it has arrived.

wrong_explanations.A: Sprint completion measures delivery pace; it is a performance indicator and can rise while security work is pushed aside.
wrong_explanations.C: Production flaws are a lagging measure; they show the risk only after it has reached live systems and customers.
wrong_explanations.D: Training completion shows attendance, not whether security work is being done or deferred in the backlog.

tips: Eliminate: A measures delivery speed, and D measures course attendance; neither tracks security risk in the work.
Final two: B beats C because a KRI should lead; deferred items show risk building, while production flaws count it after release.
Exam cue: the BEST KRI is a leading measure tied to the risk, such as a growing backlog of deferred controls.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 PO.4.1 (define criteria for software security checks, such as adding them to the Definition of Done in agile methodologies)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A5.2 (Project Risk and Agile Delivery: risk items sit in the backlog, and growing deferred security work is an early warning that risk is building). questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Choosing the first Zero Trust process
questions.question: A state lottery operator's CIO asks the risk practitioner to decide which business process moves to Zero Trust access first, as this year's budget covers one process. What is the practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Rank the processes by risk for the CIO to choose between
options.B: Pick the highest-risk process and tell the CIO its move date
options.C: Wait until funds cover moving the whole estate together
options.D: Start with the process that the product vendor suggests

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust is adopted in phases; the practitioner ranks processes by risk, and management chooses the order and funds it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the CIO asks the practitioner to do, then ask whose decision that is.
questions.correct_explanation: Sequencing a Zero Trust rollout is a funding and business decision for the CIO and the process owners; the practitioner's part is to show which processes carry the most risk and what each move would reduce. Picking the highest-risk process is the runner-up; it is a sensible rule, but the choice also weighs readiness and cost, and it belongs to those accountable for it.

wrong_explanations.B: Picking the process and date makes the practitioner the decision maker; the CIO asked, but accountability for the choice stays with management.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting to move everything together is the wholesale replacement Zero Trust guidance advises against, and it delays any risk reduction.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's suggestion may suit its product rather than the operator's risks; the order should follow the operator's own risk ranking.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for a wholesale move instead of an incremental path, and D lets the product vendor set the operator's priorities.
Final two: A beats B because the practitioner informs the choice with risk; the CIO and process owners make it.
Exam cue: when asked to decide for management, the practitioner supplies the analysis and leaves the decision with the accountable role.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 7 (Migrating to a Zero Trust Architecture: an incremental journey rather than a wholesale replacement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B1.2 (Zero Trust Architecture: adoption is incremental, and the practitioner recommends a phased, risk-prioritized path while owners fund and sequence it). questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Face recognition entry
questions.question: A co-working company plans to replace key cards with face recognition at its 30 sites, storing members' face templates in one central database. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Recognition errors that lock members out at busy times
options.B: A breach exposing members' stored face templates
options.C: Members letting guests follow them through the doors
options.D: Reliance on one vendor to hold the face templates

questions.key_concept: Biometric data cannot be reissued like a password or card, so centrally stored templates create lasting, high-impact exposure.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is new about this way of entering, then rank each harm by its impact on members.
questions.correct_explanation: A face cannot be reissued the way a key card can, and ways to revoke a stolen template are still limited. Keeping every member's template in one database means a single breach could expose all of them for good. Recognition errors are the runner-up; they would frustrate members, but a fallback such as a card or desk check can absorb them, while a stolen template cannot be undone.

wrong_explanations.A: Lockouts are a real service risk; however, a fallback entry method can absorb them, while stolen biometric data stays compromised.
wrong_explanations.C: Tailgating happens with key cards too, so it is not a risk the new technology adds.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor dependence is a commercial risk worth managing; who hosts the templates matters less than the lasting harm to members if they are stolen.

tips: Eliminate: C exists with key cards too, and D is a commercial risk; neither is a new harm the face data brings.
Final two: B beats A because a stolen face template cannot be changed; lockouts have a fallback, lasting compromise does not.
Exam cue: for biometric technology, weigh what cannot be reissued; irreversible, central exposure outranks service friction.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 (Use of Biometrics: biometric characteristics are not secrets, ways to revoke them are limited, and central storage raises privacy concerns)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A7.1 (Evaluating Emerging Technologies: identify new threats, including harms that cannot be undone such as stolen face templates). questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Technical debt deferred again
questions.question: A SaaS provider's executive committee has deferred funding for the billing platform's technical debt three years running; the CTO's requests describe only code complexity and effort. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Restate the debt as the yearly business losses it could cause
options.B: Report the debt's growth in story points to the business
options.C: Ask the CTO to resubmit with a fuller effort and cost estimate
options.D: Propose clearing the debt in engineering's spare sprint capacity

questions.key_concept: Technical debt competes for funding only when it is expressed as business impact, such as expected loss to the process it supports.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each funding request describes, then ask what the committee needs to weigh it.
questions.correct_explanation: Each request speaks engineering, and code complexity and effort cannot be weighed against other uses of the money. Restating the debt as the billing losses it could cause, such as missed invoices and delayed revenue each year, lets the committee compare the fix with its appetite and its other investments. Reporting story points is the runner-up; it shows the debt growing, but still in terms the committee cannot weigh.

wrong_explanations.B: Story points size the debt for engineers; a rising count still does not tell the committee what the business stands to lose.
wrong_explanations.C: A fuller estimate gives the committee more engineering detail, still not the business loss it needs to weigh the fix against other uses of the money.
wrong_explanations.D: Spare-capacity work sidesteps the committee's funding decision, leaves the fix unplanned, and still never shows the business loss the committee needs to weigh.

tips: Eliminate: C adds engineering detail the committee already cannot weigh, and D proposes a fix without the funding and planning management must decide.
Final two: A beats B because the committee decides in business terms; story points measure the debt, not the loss it could cause.
Exam cue: when decision makers keep deferring a technical fix, translate the risk into business impact they can weigh against appetite.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.4 (Determining Potential Impact: single loss expectancy and annualized loss expectancy); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced and removed commensurate with risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A1.3 (Technical Debt and Legacy Systems: technical debt is reported as business impact, such as expected annual loss to the process it supports, so funding decisions can weigh it against other investments). questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Training for directors
questions.question: A credit union's board asks the risk practitioner to arrange security training for its directors, who now take the same online course as all staff. What should the practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A phishing simulation aimed at each board member's inbox
options.B: The staff course again, with a certificate on completion
options.C: Hands-on training on the credit union's own security tooling
options.D: Briefings on top cyber risks and the board's oversight duty

questions.key_concept: Role-based training follows each role's risk duties; for directors that means understanding the top risks and overseeing them.
questions.pre_read: Notice who the training is for, then ask what duties that group holds that staff do not.
questions.correct_explanation: Directors share staff risks as users, which the existing course covers, but their distinct duty is oversight: approving appetite, questioning risk reports and holding management to account for cyber risk. Role-based training for them covers the top cyber risks and how to oversee them. A phishing simulation is the runner-up; directors are prime targets, but it tests a user skill rather than the board's own role.

wrong_explanations.A: Directors are frequent phishing targets; however, a simulation tests a user skill the staff course already covers, not their oversight duty.
wrong_explanations.B: Repeating the general course adds a record of completion but nothing for the duties only directors hold.
wrong_explanations.C: Tool training builds operator skills; directors oversee risk and do not run the security controls themselves.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats the general course, and C trains directors to run tools that management operates.
Final two: D beats A because role-based training targets the role's own duty; for directors that is oversight, not inbox skills.
Exam cue: role-based training follows the duties a role holds; for a board, that means understanding and overseeing the top risks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-02 (individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B2.1 (Risk-Aware Culture and Role-Based Training: role-based training gives deeper skills to people with specific risk duties, and content follows each role's risks and duties).
