questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Logging that differs by team
questions.question: Incident reviews at a telecom found that each of its 30 product teams designs its own logging, and two customer apps kept no sign-in records. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Sign-in logging added to the two apps that lack it
options.B: A logging standard set in the enterprise architecture
options.C: A logging check in each product owner's go-live review
options.D: Each product owner's acceptance of their app's logging gaps

questions.key_concept: Security requirements set in the enterprise architecture are inherited by every new design, so a gap shared by many teams is fixed at that level.
questions.pre_read: Read both findings of the incident reviews before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Logging differs by team because nothing above the teams sets what must be logged, so new apps can repeat the gaps. A logging standard in the enterprise architecture defines the events every design records, so teams build it in and the two apps are brought up to it. A go-live check is the runner-up; it needs a standard to check against and catches gaps late, one app at a time, after each design is settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding sign-in logs fixes the two apps found so far; the other teams keep designing their own logging, so new gaps keep appearing.
wrong_explanations.C: A go-live check finds gaps when they are costliest to fix and still lets 30 teams design logging their own way.
wrong_explanations.D: Owner acceptance leaves the cause in place, and gaps that weaken incident investigations across the telecom are not one product team's decision.

tips: Eliminate: A patches the two apps found so far, and D has each product owner accept gaps whose cause sits above any one team.
Final two: B beats C because a requirement set in the architecture is built into every design; a go-live check finds gaps late, one app at a time.
Exam cue: when the same control gap appears across many teams' systems, look for the architecture standard that would build the control into every design.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Evidence that a pipeline gate works
questions.question: A payments company's risk analyst is rating its CI/CD pipeline's peer-review gate, which pipeline administrators can switch off. Which of the following is the MOST reliable evidence that the gate works?

options.A: The pipeline setting that blocks merges without a second review
options.B: Engineering's report of releases that passed the gate
options.C: Each engineer's signed statement of following the review rule
options.D: Internal audit's match of sampled releases to their review records

questions.key_concept: The most reliable evidence that a control operates is an independent test of real transactions; settings show design and self-reports show intent.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the stem says the administrators can do to the gate.
questions.correct_explanation: A setting shows how the gate is designed, but administrators can switch it off, so only evidence about what was released shows whether it worked. Internal audit, independent of engineering, matching sampled releases to their review records tests the gate in operation. The pipeline setting is the runner-up; it proves the rule exists today, not that it stayed on for every release.

wrong_explanations.A: The setting shows the gate's design today; administrators can switch it off, so it says nothing about releases already made.
wrong_explanations.B: Engineering runs the gate and reports on its own work, and a count of passed releases cannot show the ones that bypassed it.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed statement records what engineers say they do, not what was released, and it comes from the people the gate checks.

tips: Eliminate: B is engineering reporting on its own gate, and C is a statement from the people the gate checks; neither tests what was released.
Final two: D beats A because a tested sample shows the gate worked on real releases; a setting that administrators can switch off shows design only.
Exam cue: to show a control operates, prefer an independent test of what actually happened, such as internal audit's sample, over settings or self-reports.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.1.1 (Notional Risk Management Roles: the auditor provides independent and formal verification of the achievement of enterprise objectives and the application of ERM processes); NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 Section 2.4.2 (Assessment Methods: examine, interview and test, with depth and coverage); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-5 (Access Restrictions for Change)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A2.3 (DevOps and Pipeline Controls: separation of duties is kept by a second person's review before merge; whoever controls the pipeline controls production; a gate is shown to work by testing real releases, such as internal audit matching a sample to review records). questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Database left after a replacement
questions.question: A theater chain replaced its ticketing system but left the database running on an unpatched cloud server with 900,000 customer records. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: A retirement phase in each project that replaces a system
options.B: An automated scan for cloud servers with no named owner
options.C: Deletion of the database and the server it runs on
options.D: The ticketing system owner's acceptance of the server risk

questions.key_concept: The SDLC ends with disposal: a replacement project retires the old data, servers and access as a planned step, so nothing keeps running unowned.
questions.pre_read: Note the goal the question sets for the recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: The database outlived the system it served, which shows retiring old components was not a planned step, so the next replacement can leave the same gap. A retirement phase in each such project names who removes or archives the old data, servers and access, and confirms it is done. An automated scan is the runner-up; it would find leftovers, but only after they have sat exposed and unpatched.

wrong_explanations.B: A scan finds leftover servers after they have sat exposed and unpatched; it detects the gap rather than closing it in each project.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing this database, once the data owner rules on keeping its records, deals with the case found; the next replacement can leave the same gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Accepting the leftover server keeps a risk the chain has no need to carry, and it does nothing to stop the next one.

tips: Eliminate: C clears this one database but not the next, and D accepts a risk that retiring the server would remove.
Final two: A beats B because a retirement phase prevents leftovers in each project; a scan only finds them after they have sat exposed.
Exam cue: when an old system outlives its replacement, the SDLC is missing its disposal phase; fix the life cycle, not only the leftover.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task M-7 (System Disposal: implement a disposal strategy and execute required actions when a system is removed from operation); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced and removed commensurate with risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A3.1 (Risk Across the SDLC Phases: disposal is planned as a project step, so the old system's data, servers and access are retired or archived and confirmed). questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Two data sets joined into one
questions.question: A retailer's analytics team joined online order records with store Wi-Fi logs, each classified internal, into one data set showing when named customers visit each store. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reuse of the internal class each source's data owner set
options.B: Access to the joined data limited to the analytics team
options.C: The data owner's class for what the joined data reveals
options.D: Removal of customer names from the joined data set

questions.key_concept: Combined data can reveal more than any source, so the data owner classifies the joined set for what it shows together, even above each source.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the joined data shows that neither source showed alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Each source is internal alone, but joined they show where and when named people go, which is more sensitive. A class for what the joined set reveals, set by the accountable data owner on the practitioner's advice, comes first, because the class sets every handling rule: access, sharing, retention and protection. Limiting access is the runner-up; chosen before the class, it is one rule and leaves sharing, retention and protection at the internal level.

wrong_explanations.A: The source classes describe each data set alone; the joined set shows customers' movements, which neither source did, so it needs its own class.
wrong_explanations.B: Limiting access is one handling rule; set before the class, it leaves sharing, retention and protection at the internal level.
wrong_explanations.D: Without names, visit times and stores can still be linked back to customers, and the joined set would still have no class of its own.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps classes that describe each source alone, and D removes names that times and places can still restore.
Final two: C beats B because the owner's class sets every handling rule; limiting access first picks one control and leaves the rest at the old level.
Exam cue: when data sets are combined, the data owner classifies the result for what it reveals together; the sources' classes are not a ceiling.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Risks kept in the project log
questions.question: A risk analyst is reviewing the risk log of a hotel group's payroll upgrade project. Which of the following risks BEST belongs only in the project's log, not the enterprise risk register?

options.A: Key developers may leave before the build is finished
options.B: The new system may go live with a weak access control
options.C: Errors in migrated records may carry into live payroll
options.D: The hosting vendor may miss its uptime target after launch

questions.key_concept: A project log holds delivery risks that end with the project; risks that continue into operation, or threaten enterprise objectives, go to the enterprise register.
questions.pre_read: Picture each risk happening, then note who would feel its effect and when.
questions.correct_explanation: A project log holds risks to delivery, which end when the project closes; developers leaving threatens the schedule and cost, then stops mattering. Risks whose effects continue in operation, or that threaten enterprise objectives, go to the enterprise register with an owner. Errors in migrated records are the runner-up; migration happens in the project, but wrong pay would keep reaching staff after go-live, so that risk outlasts the project.

wrong_explanations.B: A weak access control remains after go-live, so the risk outlasts the project and belongs with an operational owner in the enterprise register.
wrong_explanations.C: Migration happens during the project, but bad records would keep producing wrong pay after launch, so the risk reaches operations.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor uptime is an operating risk from launch onward; it belongs in the enterprise register with the payroll process owner.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe the system in use after launch, so both risks outlast the project and need an operational owner.
Final two: A beats C because developer turnover ends with delivery; migration errors start in the project but keep affecting pay afterward.
Exam cue: ask whether a risk's effect ends at project closure; if it continues into operation, or could threaten enterprise objectives, it belongs in the enterprise register.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Backup retention and hidden intruders
questions.question: A county council keeps 14 days of immutable backups, and its incident team says intruders can stay unnoticed for up to 40 days before launching ransomware. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: More frequent backups within the same 14-day window
options.B: Encryption that stops intruders reading the backups
options.C: A second immutable copy at another site for 14 days
options.D: Restore points kept longer than intruders remain hidden

questions.key_concept: Backups count only if a clean restore point exists when an attack is found, so retention should cover how long intruders may stay hidden.
questions.pre_read: Note each number in the stem and what it measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Immutable copies stop attackers changing backups, but every copy here is under 14 days old, while intruders may stay hidden for up to 40. When ransomware is found, each restore point may hold the intruders' foothold, such as planted accounts or tools. Keeping restore points beyond that period leaves a clean copy. A second immutable copy is the runner-up; it guards against losing a site, not against every copy postdating the break-in.

wrong_explanations.A: More frequent backups reduce data loss, but every copy would still be under 14 days old and could hold the intruders' foothold.
wrong_explanations.B: Encryption keeps backup data confidential; it does nothing about copies made after the intruders got in.
wrong_explanations.C: A copy at another site protects against losing one site; kept for the same 14 days, it holds the same suspect restore points.

tips: Eliminate: A changes the backup schedule, not how far back copies go, and B protects confidentiality rather than recovery.
Final two: D beats C because recovery needs a copy older than the break-in; a second site holds the same 14 days of restore points.
Exam cue: judge backup retention against how long an attack can go unnoticed; restore points taken after the break-in can bring the intruders back.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested); NIST CSF 2.0 RC.RP-03 (the integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A6.2 (Backups and Ransomware Recovery: immutable or offline copies resist an attacker with administrator access; retention must also outlast how long intruders may stay unnoticed, so a clean copy remains). Round 5, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a county council with 14 days of immutable backups against an expected 40-day hidden intrusion before ransomware) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Neighbours checked: crisc_d4_012 (contain before restoring), crisc_d4_034 (a test that never loses the online backups) and crisc_d4_035 (KCI for backups) (CRISC); CISA d4_063 (3-2-1 copies all on site), d4_162, d5_261 and d5_344 (log retention for investigations); CC cc_d2_055 (backups the domain administrators can delete). Judged distinct: none weighs backup retention against how long intruders stay hidden. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): the stem gives the incident team's estimate as an upper range ('up to 40 days'; 'in the public sector' dropped to stay within the 35-word stem limit); the explanation names the intruders' foothold (planted accounts or tools) rather than their access; key_concept and the Exam cue no longer state an absolute; notes 4A6.2 reworded. Neighbours checked: CISA d5_261 (establish when the attacker first entered before restoring) is a related dwell-time lesson at incident time rather than in retention design; judged distinct.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Scaling a pilot to every plant
questions.question: A manufacturer's private 5G pilot met every agreed condition at one plant, and operations plans to connect machines at all 14 plants next quarter under the pilot's approval. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rollout under the pilot's approval and risk assessment
options.B: A risk assessment of the network across the 14 plants
options.C: The pilot's pause conditions set at each of the 14 plants
options.D: A vendor certificate that the network supports 14 plants

questions.key_concept: A pilot's approval covers its scope; scaling an emerging technology changes exposure, so the risk is reassessed before the wider rollout.
questions.pre_read: Note the scope of the pilot and the scope of the plan.
questions.correct_explanation: The pilot's approval covered one plant. Linking machines at 14 plants to one network changes the exposure: more operations depend on it, an outage or breach can reach every plant, and integrations multiply. That needs a fresh assessment against appetite before senior management approves the rollout. Reusing the pause conditions is the runner-up; they were sized for one plant and cannot show whether the larger exposure is acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: The pilot's assessment and approval covered one plant; meeting its conditions says nothing about exposure when 14 plants depend on the network.
wrong_explanations.C: Pause conditions sized for one plant may not fit 14, and they limit losses after go-live rather than test whether the rollout is acceptable.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor certificate speaks to the product's capacity, not to the business impact of 14 plants relying on one network.

tips: Eliminate: A stretches a one-plant approval to 14 plants, and D relies on the vendor's claim about its own product.
Final two: B beats C because a larger rollout is a new exposure to assess first; pause conditions set for one plant do not size it.
Exam cue: a pilot's approval covers the pilot's scope; when an emerging technology scales up, reassess before the wider rollout.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A7.1 (Evaluating Emerging Technologies: weigh exposure against appetite, propose conditions such as a pilot, and reassess when the technology matures or a pilot scales up). Round 5, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a manufacturer scaling a one-plant private 5G pilot to all 14 plants under the pilot's approval) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Neighbours checked: crisc_d4_036 (pause conditions for a headset pilot), crisc_d4_013, crisc_d4_037, crisc_d1_066 and crisc_d3_020 (CRISC); CISA d4_245 (release before the pilot ends); CC and AAIA have no 5G or pilot scale-up item. Judged distinct: d4_036's lesson appears here only as the runner-up. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 5): explanation names senior management as approver, matching notes 4A7.1.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Two firewalls with copied rules
questions.question: A port authority guards its crane control network with two firewalls in series, both from one vendor and running a copied rule set. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: One flaw or rule error that defeats both firewalls
options.B: Rule changes made on one firewall but missed on the other
options.C: Slower crane traffic from passing through two firewalls
options.D: Support costs for keeping both firewalls under contract

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth needs layers that fail independently; two firewalls from one vendor with copied rules can be defeated by one flaw or error.
questions.pre_read: Read what the stem says about the two firewalls before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Two firewalls add depth only if they can fail independently. With one vendor and copied rules, a product flaw or a mistaken rule lets traffic through both together. A different product or rule design for one layer adds independence, but also management work and room for mistakes, so it is weighed against the risk. Rule drift is the runner-up; in series, a change missed on one firewall mostly blocks traffic rather than opening the network.

wrong_explanations.B: In series, traffic must pass both firewalls, so a change missed on one leaves the other's rule in force or blocks wanted traffic; a shared flaw opens both together.
wrong_explanations.C: Inspection by two firewalls can add delay, which is a performance matter to tune, not the gap in protection here.
wrong_explanations.D: Support costs are a budget question; they do not change how exposed the crane network is.

tips: Eliminate: C is a performance matter and D a budget one; neither describes how the crane network could be exposed.
Final two: A beats B because identical layers share one weakness; in series, drift between the copies mostly blocks traffic rather than opening the network.
Exam cue: count layers by how independently they fail; two copies of one control with the same rules are close to one layer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-29 (Heterogeneity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(2) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Supplier Diversity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B1.1 (Core Security Principles: layered controls of different kinds mean one failure does not expose the asset; layers that share a vendor, design or rule set can fail together). Round 5, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a port authority's crane control network behind two same-vendor firewalls in series with a copied rule set) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Neighbours checked: crisc_d4_053 (removing layers around customer records) and crisc_d4_015 (CRISC); CISA d5_325 (one unified appliance without a spare); CC cc_d4_009 and cc_d4_052. Judged distinct: none tests layers that share a single point of failure through the same product and rules. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): the explanation now carries SC-29's own trade-off (more diversity adds complexity and management overhead that can lead to mistakes) and says why drift is the weaker concern (in series, a missed change mostly blocks traffic); options A and D read 'both firewalls'; notes 4B1.1 bullet adds the trade-off.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Contractors outside the program
questions.question: An insurer's awareness program covers only employees; its 200 staffing-firm contractors with administrator rights take the firm's general course, which omits the insurer's policies and incident reporting. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Proof the contractors finished the staffing firm's awareness course
options.B: A contract clause making the staffing firm liable to the insurer
options.C: The business owner's acceptance of the contractors' training gap
options.D: The insurer's own security training for the contractors

questions.key_concept: Awareness reaches everyone with access, contractors included; a supplier's general course does not teach the organization's own policies, systems and reporting routes.
questions.pre_read: Notice which groups hold access and what training each one gets.
questions.correct_explanation: The contractors hold administrator rights, so the insurer stays accountable for how they use its systems. Its own security training covers what the firm's course omits: its policies and how to report a suspected incident to it, plus the duties administrator rights carry. A liability clause is the runner-up; it may recover some losses, but it moves cost, not accountability, and the contractors would still not know the insurer's rules or reporting routes.

wrong_explanations.A: Proof of the firm's course shows only that a course was taken; the stem says that course omits the insurer's policies and incident reporting, so the gap remains.
wrong_explanations.B: A liability clause may recover some losses after an incident; it moves cost, not accountability, and leaves the contractors untaught in the insurer's rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting the gap leaves 200 administrators untaught in the insurer's rules, a gap the insurer can close by training them.

tips: Eliminate: A proves completion of a course the stem says omits the insurer's rules, and C accepts a gap the insurer can readily close.
Final two: D beats B because a liability clause moves some cost but not accountability; only the insurer's own training teaches its policies and incident reporting.
Exam cue: training covers everyone with access, contractors included, and privileged users learn their extra duties; a supplier's generic course does not replace the organization's own rules.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-02 (individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind)

Judged distinct: none keys bringing a supplier's staff into the organization's own awareness program. questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Customer emails in a vendor's AI tool
questions.question: A utility's complaints team wants a vendor's AI tool to draft replies from customer emails holding names and account numbers; the vendor's terms let it train on inputs. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Removal of customer names from each email before use
options.B: Encryption of the emails as they travel to the vendor
options.C: A contract barring the vendor from training on the emails
options.D: Staff trained to check each AI-drafted reply before sending

questions.key_concept: Sharing personal data with an AI vendor keeps the organization accountable; contract terms must stop uses, such as model training, beyond the purpose of sharing.
questions.pre_read: Note what the stem says the vendor may do with the data.
questions.correct_explanation: The emails are shared to draft replies, but the vendor's terms would also let their names, account numbers and complaints train a model the utility does not control. That use goes beyond the purpose of sharing, and the utility stays accountable, so a contract barring training comes first. Removing names is the runner-up; account numbers and complaint details still identify people, and the vendor could still reuse them.

wrong_explanations.A: Removing names leaves account numbers and complaint details that still identify customers, and the vendor's terms would still let it train on them.
wrong_explanations.B: Encryption protects the emails on the way; once they arrive, the vendor's terms still allow it to train on what they contain.
wrong_explanations.D: Checking drafts guards reply quality; it does not stop the vendor training its model on the customer emails sent to it.

tips: Eliminate: B secures the emails in transit but not their later use, and D checks the replies rather than what happens to the inputs.
Final two: C beats A because the vendor's reuse is the problem; removing names still sends identifiable account data it could train on.
Exam cue: a contract term that stops an AI vendor reusing personal data prevents the harm; a liability clause only moves cost after it. The organization stays accountable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored and risk controls are applied and documented)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Standby vendor for an AI service
questions.question: A clinic's medical director adopted an AI scribe saving doctors an hour daily; typing covers outages costing $10,000 yearly, within appetite; a standby vendor costs $90,000 a year. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: A standby contract with a second AI scribe vendor
options.B: The medical director's recorded acceptance of the risk
options.C: Removal of the outage risk entry from the register
options.D: The medical director's withdrawal of the AI scribe tool

questions.key_concept: When the risk is within appetite and more recovery capacity costs more than the loss it prevents, the owner accepts on record and monitors.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the figures in the stem before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The standby vendor would cost $90,000 a year to prevent $10,000 of loss that is within appetite and limited by typing, so more treatment does not pay. The proportionate response is acceptance by the medical director, who adopted the scribe, recorded with a review date and monitored in case outages grow. Withdrawing the scribe is the runner-up; it ends the outage risk but gives up an hour a day per doctor for a small loss.

wrong_explanations.A: A standby vendor would cost $90,000 a year to prevent about $10,000 of loss; spending nine times the benefit is not a proportionate treatment.
wrong_explanations.C: An accepted risk stays in the register with its owner and is monitored; removing it means nobody would notice if the vendor's outages grew.
wrong_explanations.D: Withdrawal ends the outage risk, but it gives up an hour a day per doctor to avoid a small loss that the typing fallback already limits.

tips: Eliminate: A spends $90,000 a year to prevent $10,000 of loss, and C drops a risk from the register although accepted risks stay recorded and monitored.
Final two: B beats D because the scribe earns its keep and the loss is small; avoidance gives up that benefit, while acceptance keeps it.
Exam cue: within appetite, when treatment costs more than the loss it prevents and the technology earns its keep, expect the owner's recorded acceptance, with monitoring.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 2.1 (resources required to manage AI risks are taken into account along with viable non-AI alternative systems, approaches or methods); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost); ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance)

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Workstations that differ from the baseline
questions.question: A broadcaster's drift scans flag 20 editing workstations with USB storage on, against the baseline, because editors load camera cards; the analyzed risk is within appetite. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: USB storage blocked again on the 20 workstations
options.B: Exclusion of the editors' workstations from drift scans
options.C: Removal of the USB rule from the company-wide baseline
options.D: A recorded deviation approved by the editors' manager

questions.key_concept: A baseline deviation the business needs, with risk within appetite, is approved by its business owner, recorded and reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Note why the workstations differ from the baseline before judging the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The editors need USB storage for camera cards, and the analyzed risk is within appetite, so the deviation is accepted. On the practitioner's advice, the editors' manager, as business owner, approves it, recorded with a reason and review date, and scans keep reporting it. A lasting, limited need is reviewed periodically like an exemption, not given an exception's expiry. Excluding the machines from scans is the runner-up: it silences alerts but hides an unapproved deviation.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking USB storage again stops editors loading camera cards, a treatment the analyzed risk, already within appetite, does not call for.
wrong_explanations.B: Excluding the workstations silences the alerts, but nobody approves the deviation, and later changes on those machines would go unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Changing the company-wide baseline opens USB storage on machines with no need for it, widening the deviation far beyond the editing team.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a risk already within appetite and stops the editors' work, and C turns one team's need into a change for the whole company.
Final two: D beats B because an approved, recorded deviation is a visible acceptance decision; dropping the machines from scans removes the deviation from view instead.
Exam cue: a needed deviation within appetite is approved by the business owner, recorded and kept in monitoring, not taken out of the scans.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed)

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Archive tied to a retiring system
questions.question: Law requires a pension fund to keep member records for 60 years; it plans to retire its document system, the only software that reads the archive's format. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Conversion of the archive to a widely supported format
options.B: A retained copy of the document system, kept by its owner
options.C: Routine integrity checks on the archive in its current format
options.D: A shorter retention period agreed with the records' owner

questions.key_concept: Archived data must stay readable for its retention period, so records are converted to a supported format before the only software that reads them retires.
questions.pre_read: Note the legal requirement and the planned change before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The law sets a 60-year retention period, so the fund must still read each record long after the only software that reads the archive retires. Converting the archive to a widely supported format before retirement, and checking converted records against the originals, keeps them usable for the full period. A retained copy of the old system is the runner-up; it delays the problem but keeps retired software that must keep working for decades.

wrong_explanations.B: A copy kept by its owner keeps the retiring system alive just to read the archive for decades; the records stay locked to it.
wrong_explanations.C: Integrity checks show the files are unchanged, not that anything can still read them once the document system retires.
wrong_explanations.D: The law sets the 60-year period; the records' owner sets retention within legal limits and cannot shorten a legal minimum.

tips: Eliminate: C proves the files are unchanged but not that they can be read, and D tries to shorten a retention period that the law sets.
Final two: A beats B because conversion frees the records from one system; a kept copy of retired software must somehow keep running for decades.
Exam cue: retention means records stay usable, not just stored; before the last tool that reads a format retires, move the data to one that lasts.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components)

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Scope of a project risk log
questions.question: A city council's parking-permit app is in design, and its project risk log lists only budget, schedule and staffing risks. Which of the following should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: Key project staff leaving before the build ends
options.B: The app's launch slipping past its planned date
options.C: Unidentified risks the app will bring into operation
options.D: Project risks kept apart from the enterprise risk register

questions.key_concept: Project risk covers delivery and the risks the finished system brings into operation; both are identified early, while design can still address them.
questions.pre_read: Note what kind of risks the log holds and the project's stage.
questions.correct_explanation: Budget, schedule and staffing are delivery risks, which end when the project closes. Nothing in the log covers what the app could do once in use, such as exposing data or failing in use, and design is when controls for those risks are cheapest to build in. Keeping project risks apart from the enterprise register is the runner-up; delivery risks may stay in a project log, so separation is not the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Staff leaving is a staffing risk the log already tracks, and it ends with the build, unlike the risks the app carries into operation.
wrong_explanations.B: A late launch is a schedule risk the log already covers; it ends at closure and says nothing about the app's risks in use.
wrong_explanations.D: Delivery risks that end at closure can stay in a project log; the larger gap is that the app's operating risks are not identified at all.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are delivery risks of the kinds the log already holds, and both end when the project closes.
Final two: C beats D because separation is fine for delivery risks; the app's operating risks are missing entirely, so there is nothing yet to hand on.
Exam cue: a project risk log covers two kinds of risk, to delivery and from the finished system; budget, schedule and staffing alone miss the second.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Acceptance renewal after a platform move
questions.question: A distributor's portal owner wants to renew a 2023 acceptance of breach risk, rated within appetite before the portal moved to cloud hosting and added 12 partner APIs. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the portal's risk on its current design
options.B: Renew the owner's acceptance at the 2023 risk rating
options.C: Have the owner test the 12 partner APIs before renewal
options.D: Assess the cloud provider's own controls over the portal

questions.key_concept: An acceptance covers the risk as rated; after a major architecture change, such as a cloud move, reassess before the acceptance is renewed.
questions.pre_read: Note the dates and events in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The 2023 rating described a portal in the distributor's own hosting without the 12 partner APIs. Cloud hosting and 12 APIs change its threats and controls, so the old rating no longer shows the risk being accepted. A reassessment on the current design comes first; the owner then accepts or treats the result. Renewing at the old rating is the runner-up: it is the owner's call, but it would accept a risk nobody has rated.

wrong_explanations.B: Acceptance is the owner's decision, but within appetite holds only for the risk that was rated, and this rating predates the cloud move and the APIs.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing the APIs is one useful input for the owner, but it covers one part of the change and does not rate the portal's breach risk as a whole.
wrong_explanations.D: The provider secures its own layers; the distributor still owns its settings, data and partner links, so the provider's controls cannot rate the portal's risk.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner test only the partner links, and D looks only at the provider's side, leaving the distributor's own settings and data unrated.
Final two: A beats B because within appetite holds only for the risk that was rated; the 2023 rating predates the cloud move and the APIs.
Exam cue: an acceptance rests on its rating; when a major technology change follows the rating, reassess before the acceptance is renewed.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Assessment mitigations at launch
questions.question: Across an insurer's last five launches, the risk practitioner finds every privacy impact assessment was approved, yet a third of their mitigations were never built. What should the practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: Privacy officer sign-off on each assessment before build
options.B: A fuller assessment template with more privacy questions
options.C: A go-live check confirming each mitigation is in place
options.D: An internal audit of mitigations after each launch

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment reduces risk only when its mitigations are built, so a check before go-live confirms each one is in place.
questions.pre_read: Note what went right and what went wrong across the five launches.
questions.correct_explanation: The assessments found the privacy risks and named mitigations. The failure came later, when a third of those mitigations were never built, so the target privacy risk each owner approved, which counted those mitigations, was not the risk that went live. A go-live check that each mitigation is in place closes the gap before personal data is exposed. An internal audit after launch is the runner-up; it finds the gap only once live.

wrong_explanations.A: The assessments were already approved; another sign-off before build adds review where the process was working, not where the mitigations went missing.
wrong_explanations.B: The assessments found the risks and named mitigations; more questions improve analysis that was not the gap, and unbuilt mitigations would still go live.
wrong_explanations.D: An audit gives independent assurance, but it finds missing mitigations after launch, once people's data has already been exposed.

tips: Eliminate: A and B strengthen the assessment itself, which was approved and named the mitigations; the gap opened between approval and launch.
Final two: C beats D because a check before go-live stops a launch without its mitigations; an audit finds them missing after the exposure.
Exam cue: a privacy impact assessment helps only through mitigations that get built; look for a control between approval and launch, not a better assessment.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Change board workload
questions.question: A bank's change board spends each weekly meeting on 120 changes, mostly certificate renewals that have never failed; two outages came from complex changes it passed quickly. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A separate board meeting for certificate renewals
options.B: Pre-approval of these renewals as standard changes
options.C: A longer checklist for the changes the board reviews
options.D: Board approval waived for changes by senior engineers

questions.key_concept: Low-risk, repeatable changes with a proven record can be pre-approved as standard changes, so the change board's review time goes to riskier changes.
questions.pre_read: Note what the board reviews and what caused the outages.
questions.correct_explanation: Most of the board's time goes to renewals that have never failed, while the complex changes that caused both outages get little scrutiny. Pre-approving the renewals as standard changes, run by a tested procedure and still recorded, frees the board's attention for the risky changes. A separate meeting for renewals is the runner-up; it shortens the main meeting, but still spends review effort where the risk is lowest.

wrong_explanations.A: A separate meeting still spends reviewers' time on changes that have never failed, time that pre-approval would give to the complex changes.
wrong_explanations.C: A longer checklist adds work to each review, renewals included, without giving the complex changes more of the board's attention.
wrong_explanations.D: Seniority is not a measure of risk; waiving approval by who makes a change would let complex, risky changes skip review.

tips: Eliminate: C adds work to each review without moving time to the complex changes, and D waives approval by seniority, not by risk.
Final two: B beats A because pre-approval stops the board reviewing renewals that have never failed; a separate meeting still spends review time on them.
Exam cue: when a change board is swamped, match review effort to risk; low-risk, repeatable changes with a proven record become pre-approved standard changes.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Recording upside
questions.question: A risk analyst is drafting register entries for a supermarket chain's planned electronic shelf labels. Which of the following is BEST recorded as an opportunity?

options.A: The fixed saving from ending the paper-label print contract
options.B: Price-update checks that block unsigned changes to labels
options.C: Shoppers buying more than forecast as offers change faster
options.D: Wrong prices shown if attackers alter the label network

questions.key_concept: An opportunity is an uncertain event that would help objectives; certain, planned benefits belong in the business case, not the risk register.
questions.pre_read: Recall the ISACA meaning of opportunity before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: In ISACA's terms, an opportunity is an uncertain event that may help meet objectives. Shoppers responding to faster offers may or may not buy more than forecast, so the event is uncertain and positive, and it belongs in the register with an owner. The fixed print saving is the runner-up; it helps objectives too, but a saving known in advance carries little uncertainty and belongs in the business case.

wrong_explanations.A: Ending a known print contract gives a planned benefit, not an uncertain event; it belongs in the business case rather than the risk register.
wrong_explanations.B: Checks that block unsigned price updates are a control that treats a threat; they are recorded as a response, not as a risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Attackers altering prices is an uncertain event that would harm objectives, which makes it downside risk with the attackers as its threat, not an opportunity.

tips: Eliminate: B is a control, not an event, and D is downside risk because it would harm the chain's objectives.
Final two: C beats A because an opportunity must be uncertain; a saving known in advance is a planned benefit, not a risk.
Exam cue: risk covers uncertain upside as well as downside; an opportunity is an event that may happen and would help objectives.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (opportunity); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-07 (strategic opportunities or positive risks are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions)

Judged distinct: this keys the ISACA meaning (an uncertain positive event), with a contracted saving as the runner-up. questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Risk decisions in sprint reviews
questions.question: A bank's payments director, owning the app's risks, accepts security flaws rated within appetite in sprint reviews; the Agile team records none of the decisions. Which of the following should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: A director accepting flaws the team understands better
options.B: Risk decisions made in sprint reviews, not a committee
options.C: Security flaws accepted at release rather than fixed
options.D: Acceptances with no record of reason or review date

questions.key_concept: Agile reduces documents, not risk records: each accepted risk is still recorded with its owner, reason and review date.
questions.pre_read: Note who decides, where the decisions are made and what is kept.
questions.correct_explanation: The director owns the risks, so the acceptances are theirs to make, and a sprint review is a fair place to make them. With nothing recorded, though, no one can show what was accepted, why, or when to look again, and the flaws cannot be reported or tracked. Agile trims documents, not risk records. Accepting rather than fixing is the runner-up; acceptance by the owner is a valid response once it is recorded.

wrong_explanations.A: The team can advise on each flaw, but acceptance belongs to the risk owner, so the director deciding is the right arrangement.
wrong_explanations.B: Agile ceremonies are a sound place for risk decisions; what matters is who decides and whether the decision is recorded.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting flaws rated within appetite is a valid response for the risk owner to choose; the gap is that these acceptances leave no record to check or review.

tips: Eliminate: A would move acceptance from the risk owner to the team, and B objects to the forum, though sprint reviews can host risk decisions.
Final two: D beats C because the owner may accept flaws; what cannot be skipped is a record of what was accepted, why and until when.
Exam cue: Agile cuts heavy documents, not risk records; an accepted risk still needs a record with its reason and a review date.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Third-party articles as AI training data
questions.question: A publisher's data science team plans to train a commercial writing assistant on 40,000 news articles licensed from an agency for display on the publisher's website. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Confirmation that the license allows training the model
options.B: Removal of reporters' names from the article text
options.C: A record linking the model to each licensed article
options.D: Access to training data limited to data scientists

questions.key_concept: Holding data is not the right to train on it; the license terms are checked before third-party data trains a model.
questions.pre_read: Note the source of the training data before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The agency licensed the articles for display on the publisher's website, and training a commercial model is a different use the license may not cover. The AI RMF expects the legal risks of third-party data, including infringing others' rights, to be mapped before use, so the license is confirmed first, with legal counsel where its terms are unclear. The lineage record is the runner-up; it shows the source, not the right to use it.

wrong_explanations.B: The question is the agency's rights, not personal data; removing names leaves the licensed text in use beyond its terms.
wrong_explanations.C: Lineage records where the training data came from, which helps later, but it does not show that the license permits training.
wrong_explanations.D: Limiting access protects the articles from other staff; it does nothing about the publisher's own use beyond the license.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a rights question as a privacy one, and D controls who reads the articles, not whether training is allowed.
Final two: A beats C because a lineage record shows where the data came from; only the license terms show whether training is allowed.
Exam cue: before data trains a model, ask whether the organization has the right to use it that way, not only whether it holds the data.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Go-live with a known gap
questions.question: A car-rental firm's booking system goes live Friday without single sign-on; last week's assessment rated that launch's risk within appetite, and its design and threats are as assessed. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the risk together with the business owner
options.B: Obtain the business owner's acceptance of the risk
options.C: Record the gap as accepted in the risk register
options.D: Ask the business owner to delay go-live until sign-on is added

questions.key_concept: When a current assessment covers the facts and the risk is within appetite, the owner's acceptance comes before any new assessment.
questions.pre_read: Note what the stem says about the assessment before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Last week's assessment is current: it covers going live without single sign-on, and the design and threats are as it found them. Before go-live, the system's business owner decides whether risk within appetite is accepted or needs more treatment, so that recorded acceptance comes first, with a date to review it. Reassessing is the runner-up: it comes first after a change, but here it would repeat current work and delay the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Reassessing comes first after a change in scope, threat or controls; the design and threats are as assessed last week, so it repeats current work and delays the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: No one has accepted the gap yet; marking it accepted in the register records a decision the owner has not made, and a register records acceptance rather than making it.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk is within appetite, so holding go-live until single sign-on is added buys treatment the risk does not need; the owner can accept it and review it later.

tips: Eliminate: C lets a register entry stand in for the owner's decision, and D holds go-live to treat a risk already within appetite.
Final two: B beats A because last week's assessment covers launching without single sign-on and the design and threats are as assessed; another assessment would only delay the owner's decision.
Exam cue: reassess when the stem reports a change after the rating; when the assessment is current and the risk is within appetite and the owner's authority, the owner's decision comes next.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance); NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task R-4 (Authorization Decision: determine whether the risk from operating the system is acceptable, a decision that rests with the authorizing official)

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. An AI assistant's access to risk ratings
questions.question: A bank's AI assistant drafts the board's risk report using an account that can edit risk ratings; last quarter it lowered an owner-approved rating. What should the risk practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: Human review of each drafted report before the board sees it
options.B: An internal audit review of the AI assistant
options.C: A change history kept for the ratings the assistant edits
options.D: Read-only access to the risk ratings for the assistant

questions.key_concept: An AI tool gets only the access its task needs; an assistant that drafts reports from risk ratings should not be able to change them.
questions.pre_read: Note how the rating was changed and where that could be stopped.
questions.correct_explanation: Drafting a report needs only to read ratings, yet the assistant's account can change them, so a model error or a manipulated prompt can rewrite what an owner approved. Least privilege removes that cause: with read-only access, any rating change has to go back through its owner. Human review of each report is the runner-up: the reviewer sees a report that matches the altered rating, and the access that allowed the change stays.

wrong_explanations.A: A reviewer checks the draft against ratings that already hold the change, so the edit can pass unnoticed, and the access that allowed it remains.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives periodic assurance; a review finds the problem after the fact and leaves the access that causes it in place.
wrong_explanations.C: A change history shows edits after they happen and helps only if someone reads it; the assistant can still change ratings that owners approved.

tips: Eliminate: B gives assurance after the fact without removing the access, and C records edits the assistant can still make.
Final two: D beats A because a reviewer compares the draft with ratings that already hold the change; removing the edit right stops it at its source.
Exam cue: when a person or AI tool holds access its task does not need, remove the access before adding reviews or logs around it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Restore tests and the ransomware playbook
questions.question: A manufacturer's restore tests recover its planning system in six hours, inside its 12-hour RTO, but its ransomware playbook needs two days of containment and malware checks first. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: A ransomware recovery lasting far longer than the RTO
options.B: Ransomware coming back with data restored from backups
options.C: Planning data lost since the last backup beyond the RPO
options.D: A six-hour restore leaving too little margin in the RTO

questions.key_concept: Recovery time under ransomware includes containment and clean checks, so a restore test alone can overstate how fast a system would return.
questions.pre_read: Note every step the stem describes and how long each takes.
questions.correct_explanation: The restore test times only the restore. In a ransomware attack, the playbook adds two days of containment and checks before restoring starts, so recovery would take about 54 hours against a 12-hour RTO. That gap, in the scenario that matters most for recovery, is what the process owner needs to see. Reinfection from backups is the runner-up: it is a real ransomware risk, but the playbook's malware checks exist to address it.

wrong_explanations.B: Reinfection is a real ransomware risk, but the playbook already requires malware checks before any restore; the exposure the checks leave open is time, not reinfection.
wrong_explanations.C: The RPO limits how much data may be lost; the stem gives no backup interval or data loss, and the shortfall it shows is in recovery time.
wrong_explanations.D: A six-hour restore against a 12-hour RTO meets the target with time to spare; the margin is not the problem, the steps before the restore are.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps recovery time for data loss, which the stem never mentions, and D worries about a margin the tested restore already meets.
Final two: A beats B because the playbook's checks already address reinfection; what they leave open is a recovery far longer than the RTO.
Exam cue: judge recovery capability by the full timeline of the scenario that matters, not by the one step a test happens to time.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (recovery time objective); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-01 (incidents are contained); NIST CSF 2.0 RC.RP-03 (the integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration)

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. What a privacy impact assessment rates
questions.question: A dating service's privacy impact assessment for a feature showing members' location to their matches rates each risk only by the fines and press coverage it would face. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Fine estimates updated from recent enforcement cases
options.B: A penetration test of the feature before launch
options.C: Ratings that also count members who leave the service
options.D: Ratings that start from the harm that members could suffer

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment rates the problems processing could cause people first, then the impacts that follow for the organization.
questions.pre_read: Note what the assessment's ratings measure before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy risk is the chance that people suffer problems from how their data is processed. Showing members' location to their matches could lead to stalking or physical harm; fines and press coverage are costs that follow for the service. Rating harm to members first, then the service's impacts, shows the owner the real exposure. Counting members who leave is the runner-up: it is one more cost to the service and still omits the harm.

wrong_explanations.A: Sharper fine estimates refine the same narrow measure; a feature can be lawful and still expose members to stalking, which no fine figure captures.
wrong_explanations.B: The harm comes from the feature working as designed; a penetration test looks for security flaws, not the risk of showing members' location.
wrong_explanations.C: Members leaving is a cost to the service that follows from harm; adding it keeps every rating on the service's losses and still omits the harm to members.

tips: Eliminate: A sharpens the fine estimates the ratings already use, and B tests for security flaws when the harm comes from the feature working as designed.
Final two: D beats C because members leaving is still a cost to the service; a privacy assessment rates the problems for the people first, then the costs that follow.
Exam cue: privacy risk starts with the people whose data is processed; fines, lost customers and press coverage follow from their harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 Section 1.2.1 Figure 3 (Relationship Between Privacy Risk and Organizational Risk: individuals experience the direct impact of problems from data processing, and organizational impacts such as noncompliance costs, customer abandonment and reputational harm follow); NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 ID.RA-P (Risk Assessment: the organization understands the privacy risks to individuals and how they may create follow-on impacts on organizational operations); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-8 (Privacy Impact Assessments)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Choosing awareness topics
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner recommend as the BEST basis for choosing next year's security awareness topics at a toy maker?

options.A: The phishing scenarios in a ready-made training catalog
options.B: The topics staff rated most useful in last year's feedback
options.C: The top-rated risk scenarios that depend on staff actions
options.D: The cyber risks named most often in this year's industry reports

questions.key_concept: Awareness topics follow the organization's risk profile, starting with the highest-rated scenarios that depend on what staff do.
questions.pre_read: Compare where each option's topics would come from before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness is a control, so its topics should follow the organization's own risk profile: the highest-rated scenarios where what staff do changes likelihood or impact, such as payment diversion or mishandled customer data. That puts limited training time where it reduces the most risk. Industry reports are the runner-up: they keep content current and inform the ratings, but they describe other organizations' exposure, not what matters most at this toy maker.

wrong_explanations.A: A ready-made catalog is written for every customer; it may cover phishing well and still miss the scenarios rated highest at this firm.
wrong_explanations.B: Topics staff enjoy keep them engaged, but what staff find useful is not a measure of where their actions drive the firm's risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Industry reports show what attackers do in general; they feed the firm's ratings but do not say which scenarios matter most here.

tips: Eliminate: A takes topics from a ready-made general catalog, and B lets staff preference set them; neither starts from this firm's risks.
Final two: C beats D because industry reports describe threats in general; the firm's own rated scenarios show where staff behavior changes its risk most.
Exam cue: training, like any control, is aimed by the organization's own risk profile; outside sources feed the profile but do not replace it.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Accepting an unsupported server's risk
questions.question: A refinery director, who may accept up to $250,000, wants to accept an unsupported server's $400,000 exposure within appetite and tolerance; its setup and threats are as assessed. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the server's $400,000 exposure before the director accepts it
options.B: Have the director accept it on record with a review date
options.C: Refer it to an executive whose authority covers $400,000
options.D: Propose an upgrade that brings the exposure under $250,000

questions.key_concept: Acceptance needs an exposure within appetite and tolerance and a signer whose delegated authority covers that exposure.
questions.pre_read: List every limit the stem gives, and whom each one binds, before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The server's setup and threats are as assessed and the exposure is within appetite and tolerance, so acceptance is a valid response and no reassessment is due. But acceptance must come from someone whose delegated authority covers the exposure, and the director's stops at $250,000. The practitioner refers the decision to an executive who holds that authority. Recorded acceptance by the director is the runner-up: right within the director's limit, not above it.

wrong_explanations.A: The setup and threats are as assessed, so a new assessment repeats current work; the open question is who may accept a $400,000 exposure, not what it is.
wrong_explanations.B: Recorded acceptance with a review date fits an exposure within the signer's authority; this one is $400,000, and the director may accept only up to $250,000.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk is within appetite and tolerance, so no treatment is required; spending to fit a signer's limit puts cost ahead of the decision an authorized executive should make.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats an assessment that still matches the server and its threats, and D funds treatment for a risk within appetite and tolerance only to fit a signing limit.
Final two: C beats B because acceptance within appetite and tolerance still needs a signer whose delegated authority covers the exposure; the director's authority stops at $250,000.
Exam cue: before keying owner acceptance, check appetite and tolerance, then the signer's delegated authority; an exposure above that authority goes to someone who holds it.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. A scheduled fix and a workaround
questions.question: A city council's problem team traced repeated permit-system outages to a software flaw; the fix ships in March, and an owner-approved workaround keeps the risk within appetite. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Escalate the March fix date to the system's risk owner
options.B: Monitor the workaround's results until the fix ships
options.C: Ask IT, as system owner, to sign an acceptance of the risk
options.D: Ask the owner to rush the fix as an emergency change

questions.key_concept: Once the owner has chosen a response and risk sits within appetite, the practitioner monitors it and escalates only when a trigger is met.
questions.pre_read: Note which decisions the stem says are already made, and by whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The cause is known, the fix has a release date, and the workaround the owner approved holds the risk within appetite, so the response is decided. The practitioner's part now is monitoring: checking that the workaround keeps outages contained and that the fix lands in March, and raising it if either slips. Escalating to the risk owner is the runner-up: the owner has already decided, so escalation adds no decision while risk stays within appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner approved the workaround and the risk is within appetite; escalation suits a breach or a slipped date, and neither has happened yet.
wrong_explanations.C: IT runs the system but does not own the outage risk; the business owner has already approved the workaround, so no acceptance is needed from IT.
wrong_explanations.D: Emergency changes are for needs that cannot wait; with the owner's approved workaround holding risk within appetite, the fix can follow normal release testing.

tips: Eliminate: C asks IT to accept a risk it does not own, and D sends a fix that can wait through the emergency path, skipping normal release testing.
Final two: B beats A because the owner has already decided and the risk is within appetite; the practitioner watches for a slip and escalates only then.
Exam cue: when the owner has chosen a response and risk sits within appetite, the practitioner's move is monitoring against a trigger, not escalating again.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Research data without a class
questions.question: A research hospital's genomics team has gathered patient sequencing data for three months and plans to classify it next year, before sharing it with a university partner. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data owner classify the data set now
options.B: Have the data owner classify it before the partner share
options.C: Encrypt the data set until the partner share is approved
options.D: Have IT classify the data set as its custodian

questions.key_concept: Data is classified by its owner when it is created or collected, because the class sets every later handling rule.
questions.pre_read: Compare when each option would put handling rules in place.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification sets the handling rules for data, such as who may access it, how it is stored and how long it is kept, so the owner assigns it when data is created or collected. This data set has held patient information for three months with no class. Classifying before the partner share is the runner-up: the share does need a class, but the exposure began when the data was gathered, not when it leaves.

wrong_explanations.B: The owner is right but the timing is not: the data has sat unclassified for three months, and storage and access inside the team already need rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption is one handling rule; without a class, nobody has decided who may access the data, how long it is kept or how it may be shared.
wrong_explanations.D: IT applies handling rules as custodian; setting the class belongs to the data owner, who answers for how the data is used.

tips: Eliminate: C picks one control before anyone has set the data's class, and D gives the class decision to IT, which only applies the owner's rules.
Final two: A beats B because the class sets handling from the moment data exists; waiting for the share leaves months of patient data without rules.
Exam cue: data is classified by its owner when it is created or collected; a later event such as sharing is a reason to review the class, not to set it.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Security tests cut to meet a date
questions.question: To meet a regulator's date, a gas supplier's program board cut its billing app's last-sprint security tests, and the app owner accepted the risk without an estimate. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The program board overruling the security team's plan
options.B: Acceptance given with the app's flaws still unknown
options.C: The team's sprint velocity falling below its plan
options.D: Higher cost of fixing flaws found after launch

questions.key_concept: Acceptance is valid only for an analyzed risk; an owner who accepts a risk nobody has estimated has not made an informed decision.
questions.pre_read: Read each concern as a problem in its own right, then rank them.
questions.correct_explanation: An acceptance is only as sound as the analysis behind it. The cut tests were how the app's flaws would be found, and the owner accepted without an estimate, so nobody can say whether the risk is within appetite; the practitioner asks for one before launch. The board overruling the security team's plan is the runner-up: boards may trade scope for a date, but the decision then needs an analyzed risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A program board may trade scope for a date when the owner is informed; the plan changing matters less than an acceptance resting on no estimate.
wrong_explanations.C: Velocity measures delivery pace, a performance measure; it says nothing about the size of the security risk the cut tests left unknown.
wrong_explanations.D: Later fixes do cost more, but that cost is secondary; the larger issue is a risk of unknown size accepted for launch.

tips: Eliminate: C tracks delivery pace rather than risk, and D weighs the cost of later fixes while the size of the risk itself is unknown.
Final two: B beats A because a board may trade scope for a date; what makes this decision unsound is acceptance with no estimate behind it.
Exam cue: acceptance needs an analyzed risk to compare with appetite; when the work that measures the risk is cut, ask for an estimate before go-live.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. A digital twin with remote control
questions.question: A dairy plans a digital twin of its pasteurizing line, hosted on a start-up's cloud platform, through which engineers could change heating settings remotely. Which of the following should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: The start-up failing and the line's model being lost
options.B: Unsafe heating changes made through the cloud platform
options.C: Sensor data showing the dairy's milk output volumes
options.D: Cloud storage costs rising as sensor data builds up

questions.key_concept: A new path from a cloud service to physical process controls adds safety and integrity risk that outranks data and vendor concerns.
questions.pre_read: Picture the worst realistic outcome of each option before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: A cloud path that can change heating settings links an internet-hosted service to the physical process that makes milk safe, so an error or misuse could put unsafe product on shelves, not just expose data. That safety and integrity exposure outweighs the others. The start-up failing is the runner-up: losing the twin's model costs money and insight, but the line keeps pasteurizing without it, while a misused control path could make the milk unsafe.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor failure is a real risk with a start-up and calls for exit terms, but the line runs without its twin; lost analytics cost less than unsafe milk.
wrong_explanations.C: Output volumes are low-sensitivity operating data; exposing them has a small impact beside a path that can change how the line heats milk.
wrong_explanations.D: Rising storage cost is a budgeting matter the business case can cover; it does not threaten safe operation of the line.

tips: Eliminate: C exposes low-sensitivity operating data, and D is a cost the business case can cover; neither touches the safety of the product.
Final two: B beats A because the line keeps pasteurizing if the start-up fails, but a misused remote control path could make the milk unsafe.
Exam cue: when new technology links an internet service to a physical process, rank threats to safety and integrity above data and vendor concerns.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 3.2.1 (Benefits of Cybersecurity Investments: cyber attacks on OT can have physical impacts, particularly personal injury and loss of life, and damage to the environment); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 6.2.10 (Remote Access: provide remote access to OT only if justified and limited to the business need, and never so that it circumvents safety or security controls)

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Requirements reused from an earlier product
questions.question: A game studio's team for its first online multiplayer title, now in design, has copied the security requirements of its last game, which ran offline. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Requirements set from the new game's own risk assessment
options.B: The product owner's sign-off on the copied requirements
options.C: Requirements taken from the studio's secure coding checklist
options.D: A security assessment the business owner orders after beta

questions.key_concept: Security requirements come from a risk assessment of the system being built; requirements copied from a different system miss its own threats.
questions.pre_read: Compare where each option gets its requirements and at what stage it acts.
questions.correct_explanation: Security requirements should come from the risks of the system being built. An online multiplayer game faces threats an offline game never did, such as account takeover, cheating, payment fraud and attacks on its servers, so its own risk assessment, done now in design, sets them. The secure coding checklist is the runner-up: it is a sound baseline against common coding flaws, but it is generic and cannot name this game's threats.

wrong_explanations.B: Sign-off approves the list but does not make it fit; requirements written for an offline game still miss the online game's threats.
wrong_explanations.C: A secure coding checklist is a useful baseline, but it covers common flaws in code, not the threats specific to an online multiplayer game.
wrong_explanations.D: An assessment after beta finds gaps once the design is built, when fixes cost most; requirements belong in design, before the build.

tips: Eliminate: B has the owner approve requirements written for a different product, and D assesses after beta, once the design is built and fixes cost most.
Final two: A beats C because a generic coding checklist is only a baseline, while the game's own risk assessment finds threats an offline game never faced.
Exam cue: when a project reuses another system's requirements or controls, ask what is new about this system; its requirements follow its own assessed risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 PW.1.1 (use forms of risk modeling, such as threat modeling, attack modeling or attack surface mapping, to help assess the security risk for the software); NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task P-14 (Risk Assessment for the System: conduct a system-level risk assessment from initiation and update it on an ongoing basis)
