questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Where backup keys are kept
questions.question: A chemical distributor encrypts the backups it sends offsite, and the only copy of the decryption keys sits in a key vault at its main data center. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: An intruder at the main site using the keys to read backups
options.B: Restores slowed by decrypting backups at the recovery site
options.C: Offsite backups left unreadable if the main site is lost
options.D: Staff at the offsite store reading the backup media

questions.key_concept: Offsite backups must survive the loss of the main site, so the keys that decrypt them are kept apart from it but reachable in recovery.
questions.pre_read: For each option, picture the event that would cause it and what it would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Offsite backups exist for the day the main site is lost. With the only decryption keys in a vault at that site, the fire, flood or ransomware attack that takes the data center also locks every offsite copy, and recovery fails. Keys belong apart from the site yet reachable. An intruder reading backups is the runner-up: someone inside the main site can already reach the live data, so the backups add little exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: An intruder inside the main site can already reach the live data; reading the backups adds little beside losing every backup in a disaster.
wrong_explanations.B: Decryption adds some restore time, but that is a performance cost; once the keys are gone, the backups cannot be restored at all.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption with the keys held elsewhere is what stops offsite staff reading the media; this is the design's strength, not its gap.

tips: Eliminate: B is a small performance cost rather than a recovery gap, and D is the risk the encryption already handles, since the offsite store never holds the keys.
Final two: C beats A because an intruder at the main site can already reach the live data, while losing that site would leave every offsite backup unreadable.
Exam cue: test a recovery design against the loss of the main site; anything recovery needs, such as keys, credentials or runbooks, must not exist only there.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 5.1.2 (Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup: key management keeps encrypted backups available, with keys stored separate from, but accessible to, the backup data); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-12(1) (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management | Availability)

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. What Zero Trust access changes
questions.question: A courier firm's depot applications now sit behind tested Zero Trust access that checks the user and device in each session. Which register scenario's rating should the risk practitioner expect to fall MOST?

options.A: An intruder using one stolen login to reach other systems
options.B: A driver misusing customer addresses within their job access
options.C: A cloud outage taking the depot applications offline
options.D: Depot staff mistyping parcel details that misroute deliveries

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust removes trust based on network location, so its largest effect is on lateral movement from a compromised account or device.
questions.pre_read: Match each scenario to the kind of control that would change its likelihood or impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust grants no trust for network location and checks the user and device in each session, so an intruder with one stolen login can no longer move freely from system to system; NIST SP 800-207 says this stops compromised accounts moving laterally. A driver misusing permitted addresses is the runner-up: the checks confirm a valid driver on a valid device, so access the job grants is still allowed.

wrong_explanations.B: Per-session checks confirm a valid driver on a valid device; misuse of addresses the job allows passes them, so this rating moves little.
wrong_explanations.C: Zero Trust governs who may connect, not whether the cloud service runs; its policy service can even add a dependency for availability.
wrong_explanations.D: Typing errors by authorized staff happen inside permitted access; input checks, not access decisions, change this rating.

tips: Eliminate: C is an availability event that access checks cannot prevent, and D is an error by authorized staff that input controls, not access decisions, address.
Final two: A beats B because a valid driver on a valid device passes every check, while a stolen login can no longer move freely from system to system.
Exam cue: Zero Trust cuts the reach of a compromised account or device; it does little against outages, honest errors or misuse within granted access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust: network location alone does not imply trust, and access to each enterprise resource is granted per session); NIST SP 800-207 Section 5.3 (Stolen Credentials/Insider Threat: Zero Trust stops compromised accounts or assets from moving laterally, but a valid account can still reach the resources it is granted)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Staff reading of an AI-use rule
questions.question: A print works survey shows staff know AI image tools are for non-confidential work only, but most class unreleased customer artwork, marked confidential by policy, as non-confidential. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A policy reminder that AI is for non-confidential work
options.B: AI-use training with examples of confidential customer files
options.C: A manager's sign-off before confidential customer files reach AI tools
options.D: A block on AI image tools across the print works network

questions.key_concept: Awareness must show what a rule means in practice; staff apply a rule like 'non-confidential only' through their own idea of confidential.
questions.pre_read: Read the survey result before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff already know the rule; they misjudge what it covers, treating unreleased artwork as safe to upload. Training with concrete examples of confidential customer files, such as unreleased designs, corrects that belief where the decision is made. A policy reminder is the runner-up: it repeats the rule, but staff who think unreleased artwork is non-confidential will read the reminder the same way and keep uploading it.

wrong_explanations.A: Repeating the rule leaves its meaning unchanged; staff who think unreleased artwork is non-confidential will keep uploading it while following the reminder.
wrong_explanations.C: Sign-off catches only files staff already see as confidential; those who think unreleased artwork is not will never ask for it.
wrong_explanations.D: A ban ends an approved use and tends to push staff to personal devices, without teaching what counts as confidential.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a sign-off that staff who misjudge artwork will never seek, and D bans an approved use, which tends to drive it onto personal devices.
Final two: B beats A because staff already know the rule; a reminder repeats words they misread, while examples change what they think the rule covers.
Exam cue: when staff break a rule they know, find what they misunderstand; awareness built on concrete examples beats repeating the policy.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Order histories for a partner's AI model
questions.question: A food-delivery platform's app will take orders only from customers who agree that their order histories may train a partner's AI advertising model. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A clearer privacy notice explaining the training use
options.B: A security review of the AI partner's data controls
options.C: A contract making the AI partner liable for data misuse
options.D: Separate, optional consent for the AI model training

questions.key_concept: Consent is valid only as a real choice; tying an unrelated use, such as AI training, to the core service leaves customers none.
questions.pre_read: Decide what privacy problem the stem describes before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Ordering food does not need a partner's AI advertising model, yet customers must accept that use to order at all, so their agreement is not a real choice. Making consent to the training separate and optional lets customers order and still decline it. A clearer notice is the runner-up: it tells customers plainly what happens, but they still cannot order without agreeing, so the consent stays forced.

wrong_explanations.A: Plain wording informs customers, but agreement is still a condition of ordering; telling people more does not give them a choice.
wrong_explanations.B: A security review protects the shared data from others; it does not change whether customers freely agreed to the training use.
wrong_explanations.C: Liability shifts some cost to the partner after misuse; customers must still accept the training use to place an order.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a privacy problem as a security one, and C moves the cost of misuse; neither changes what customers must accept to order.
Final two: D beats A because a clearer notice explains the training use but keeps it a condition of ordering; only separating it gives customers a choice.
Exam cue: when an extra use of personal data is tied to the core service, the privacy answer unbundles it so people can refuse and still be served.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Unpatched controllers awaiting replacement
questions.question: A semiconductor fab's lithography controllers run an operating system the vendor no longer patches; replacement is due in 2029, and their analyzed risk is above appetite. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Acceptance of the risk by the lithography process owner
options.B: Vulnerability scans of the controllers, reported to the process owner
options.C: Isolation of the controllers on a separate network segment
options.D: A request that the process owner raise the risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Unpatchable legacy technology needs a compensating control, such as isolation, until replacement; finding flaws no one can fix lowers nothing.
questions.pre_read: Note where the rating sits against appetite and what the vendor still provides.
questions.correct_explanation: With no patches coming and replacement years away, the risk above appetite must be treated now. Isolating the controllers on a separate segment removes most routes an attacker could use to reach them; NIST SP 800-53 SA-22 names isolation as a way to reduce the risk of unsupported components. Vulnerability scans are the runner-up: they show which flaws exist, but none can be patched, so the exposure stays above appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: An owner may accept risk within appetite; this rating is above it, so the process owner cannot accept it, and the exposure would continue as it is.
wrong_explanations.B: Scans list the controllers' flaws, but the vendor issues no patches, so the findings cannot be fixed and the exposure stays where it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management and the board set risk appetite; a process owner cannot raise it, and loosening the limit to fit one risk does not reduce that risk.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both turn to the process owner, who can accept only risk within appetite and cannot change appetite, which senior management and the board set.
Final two: C beats B because scans find flaws that no patch will fix, while isolation cuts the routes an attacker would use until the 2029 replacement.
Exam cue: when legacy technology cannot be patched and its risk is above appetite, look for a compensating control that reduces exposure, not more ways to watch it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced and removed commensurate with risk)

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. A change that broke an unlisted system
questions.question: A smart-building operator tested a sign-in server change with the staff portal, the only dependent system its impact assessment named, yet badge readers in 40 buildings failed. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Each item's links to other systems recorded in the CMDB
options.B: A tested back-out plan for each sign-in server change
options.C: Change board approval for each change to shared systems
options.D: Scheduling of sign-in server changes for weekends

questions.key_concept: A change impact assessment is only as complete as its configuration records; the CMDB should link each item to the systems relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the testing missed the failure before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The test and the impact assessment covered only what the team knew relied on the server, so the root cause is missing configuration records. Recording each item's links to other systems in the CMDB lets the next impact assessment find the badge readers before the change. A tested back-out plan is the runner-up: it shortens the next outage, but the readers would still fail first, because no one would know they rely on the server.

wrong_explanations.B: A back-out plan restores service faster after a failure; it does not tell the team beforehand that the badge readers rely on the server.
wrong_explanations.C: The board judges a change from its impact assessment; one that names only the staff portal would lead the board to the same approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Weekend timing reduces how many people a failure affects, but the readers still rely on the server and would fail again.

tips: Eliminate: C adds an approval that rests on the same incomplete impact assessment, and D moves the change's timing without showing which systems rely on the server.
Final two: A beats B because a back-out plan recovers after the readers fail, while recorded links let the impact assessment foresee the failure.
Exam cue: when a change breaks a system nobody listed, fix the configuration records the impact assessment draws on before adding approvals or recovery steps.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-128 Section 3.1.2 (Planning at the System Level: the system component inventory can record each component's relationships to and dependencies on other systems, and adds value when it supports security impact analysis of changes); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)

Judged distinct: no bank item keys dependency records in the CMDB as the fix for a change that broke an unlisted system, and the final two is prevention through configuration records against a back-out plan.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Customer phone copies kept after repair
questions.question: An electronics repair chain copies each customer's phone to a store PC before repair in case it is wiped; copies from 2021 remain. Which deletion point should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Seven years, the period the chain keeps its invoices
options.B: Whenever a store PC's disk nears its capacity
options.C: Once the repaired phone is handed back with its data restored
options.D: When the customer asks the chain to delete their phone copy

questions.key_concept: Data copied for a short task is deleted when the task ends; retention follows purpose, not storage space, other records' periods or customer requests.
questions.pre_read: Work out why the copies exist before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The copies exist only to protect customers' data if a repair wipes the phone, so their purpose ends once the phone is handed back with the data restored. Deleting then, under a rule the chain's data owner sets, stops personal data piling up. Deletion on request is the runner-up: it honors a customer's wish, but copies nobody asks about, like those from 2021, would stay for good.

wrong_explanations.A: Invoices are kept for legal and tax reasons; phone copies serve only the repair, so tying them to another record's period keeps personal data for years without need.
wrong_explanations.B: Disk space measures storage, not need; copies would stay as long as space allows, so a roomy PC would keep customers' data for years.
wrong_explanations.D: A deletion request must be honored, but retention should end when the purpose does; copies nobody asks about, like those from 2021, would stay for good.

tips: Eliminate: A borrows the invoice period, set for other records and reasons, and B lets disk space decide how long personal data is kept.
Final two: C beats D because a copy's purpose ends when the phone goes back with its data; waiting for requests keeps copies nobody asks about.
Exam cue: tie retention to the purpose the data was collected for; when the purpose ends, so does the reason to keep it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); ISACA Glossary (data owner)

An earlier legal-hold angle for this slot was dropped as a mirror of cc_d5_021. Judged distinct: no bank item covers short-task copies of customer devices, and the final two is a deletion point set by the data owner against encrypting data that should no longer be kept. questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. A project whose customer has left
questions.question: A satellite operator's ground station, being built for a maritime customer who has since canceled, is 70% complete; its sponsor wants to finish it because $9,000,000 is spent. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Analyze the delivery risks in the project's risk log
options.B: Back the sponsor's plan to complete the ground station
options.C: Stop the project's spending until a new customer signs
options.D: Bring the project's new value and risk to the portfolio board

questions.key_concept: Continuing a project rests on the value and risk of the remaining spend; a project whose value has gone returns to the portfolio board.
questions.pre_read: Note what has changed about the project before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The customer the station was built for has gone, so the value that justified the project has changed, and continuing or stopping it is a portfolio decision. The practitioner brings the changed value and risk to the portfolio board so it decides on the money still to be spent. Analyzing delivery risks is the runner-up: it is sound analysis, but delivery is not what changed, and the project log keeps the decision inside the project.

wrong_explanations.A: Delivery risks cover building the station on time and budget; what changed is its value, and the project log does not take that to the decision makers.
wrong_explanations.B: Money already spent is gone whichever way the decision goes; continuing should rest on the value and risk of the spend still to come.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping an approved project's spending is a portfolio decision; the practitioner supplies the risk view and does not halt the project on their own.

tips: Eliminate: B lets money already spent decide the future, which portfolio reviews avoid, and C has the practitioner halt an approved project, a decision for the portfolio board.
Final two: D beats A because the change is to the project's value, not its delivery; the portfolio board, not the project log, decides on the remaining spend.
Exam cue: when a project's business case falls away, take the changed value and risk to whoever governs the portfolio; money already spent is no reason to continue.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); ISACA Now Blog 23 September 2019 (IT risk has three categories: benefit/value enablement, program and project delivery, and operations and service delivery)

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Pickup records on a public blockchain
questions.question: A parcel-locker network plans to record each pickup, with the recipient's name and locker location, on a public blockchain as tamper-evident delivery records. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Attackers rewriting pickup records already on the chain
options.B: Personal data on a public ledger that cannot be erased
options.C: Pickup errors kept on a ledger that cannot be edited
options.D: One server outage taking the public ledger offline

questions.key_concept: Public blockchain records are readable by anyone and cannot be removed, so personal data written there stays exposed and cannot be erased.
questions.pre_read: Read the plan's details closely before ranking the four concerns.
questions.correct_explanation: On a public (permissionless) blockchain anyone can read the records, and entries cannot be removed, so each recipient's name and locker location would stay exposed for good, with no way to honor a deletion request. Kept errors are the runner-up: a wrong pickup record cannot be edited, but a later entry can correct it, while personal data once published cannot be taken back.

wrong_explanations.A: Public blockchains are built to be tamper-evident and tamper-resistant; rewriting confirmed records needs most of the network's resources, which is costly and hard to hide.
wrong_explanations.C: A wrong record stays on the chain, but a new entry can correct or supersede it; published personal data cannot be recalled that way.
wrong_explanations.D: A blockchain ledger is copied across many independent nodes, so one server failing does not take the ledger offline.

tips: Eliminate: A overrates the threat to records already on the chain, which resist tampering, and D treats the ledger as one server when copies run on many nodes.
Final two: B beats C because an error can be corrected by a later entry, but names and locations published to everyone can never be withdrawn.
Exam cue: with emerging technology, weigh most heavily the harm that cannot be reversed; a feature like permanence can turn personal data into a lasting exposure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8202 Section 8.1 (Additional Blockchain Considerations: data on a permissionless blockchain is generally public, personal data may not be appropriate to store, and records can be amended by new transactions but not removed)

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). A flaw report from outside the firm
questions.question: A researcher's two emails to a legal-tech start-up's support inbox about a flaw exposing clients' contracts went unanswered, so the researcher published it. What should the risk practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: Support staff training on flaw reports, set up by the product owner
options.B: Legal action the business owner approves against researchers
options.C: A fixed patch deadline for each critical flaw once reported
options.D: A public route for outside flaw reports, with set reply times

questions.key_concept: Outsiders will find flaws that no test caught; a public route for their reports, with roles and reply times, turns a warning into a fix.
questions.pre_read: Work out where the process broke before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The warning reached a general support inbox where no one handled flaw reports, so the flaw went public unfixed. A public route for flaw reports, with set reply times, brings outside warnings to the people who fix them; NIST's SSDF calls for a disclosure policy with roles and processes. Training support staff is the runner-up: it may catch the next report, but leaves reports in a general inbox with no known route or reply duty.

wrong_explanations.A: Trained staff may spot the next report, but flaw reports would still land in a general inbox, with no known route for researchers and no reply time.
wrong_explanations.B: Threatening researchers discourages the very reports the start-up needs, and the flaw stays in place; disclosure programs invite reports instead of punishing them.
wrong_explanations.C: A patch deadline starts once the start-up knows about a flaw; this one sat unanswered in a support inbox, so no deadline would ever have started.

tips: Eliminate: B deters the researchers whose reports the start-up needs, and C sets a patch deadline that starts only after someone reads the report.
Final two: D beats A because training leaves flaw reports in a general inbox with no owner or reply time; a public route gives them both.
Exam cue: when an outside warning goes unanswered, give warnings a defined route, owner and reply time; training whoever happened to receive one leaves the gap open.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 RV.1.3 (have a policy that addresses vulnerability disclosure and remediation, and implement the roles, responsibilities and processes needed to support it); NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 RV.1.1 (gather information from software acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities and investigate all credible reports)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. A navigation model kept at one site
questions.question: A warehouse robotics firm's servers recover within the 8-hour RTO, but the robots' navigation model, stored only at the main site, would take three weeks to retrain. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep offsite copies of each model version its owner releases
options.B: Test whether the recovery site can restore the model
options.C: Have the model owner sign off each retrained model version
options.D: Ask the operations owner to fund faster retraining hardware

questions.key_concept: A trained AI model is a recovery asset like data; keep versioned copies offsite, because retraining takes far longer than a restore.
questions.pre_read: List what the robots need to work again before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The servers return within the RTO, but the robots cannot work without the navigation model, and rebuilding it takes three weeks. A trained model is a recovery asset like data: offsite copies of each released version can be restored within hours. Testing whether the recovery site can restore the model is the runner-up: the model exists only at the main site, so a test would confirm the gap without closing it.

wrong_explanations.B: A test would only confirm what is already known: the model exists only at the main site, so the recovery site has nothing to restore.
wrong_explanations.C: Sign-off controls which model versions go live; it does nothing to make a released model available if the main site is lost.
wrong_explanations.D: Faster hardware might cut retraining from weeks to days, still far beyond the 8-hour RTO, while a stored copy restores within hours.

tips: Eliminate: C governs which model versions go live, not how one is recovered, and D still rebuilds the model in days when the RTO allows 8 hours.
Final two: A beats B because the gap is already known: the model sits only at the main site, so a test would confirm the failure, not fix it.
Exam cue: list everything a process needs to run again, trained AI models included; anything that cannot be restored within the RTO is a gap to close, not to retest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Rating an encrypted contract archive
questions.question: An e-signature provider's register rates its encrypted signed-contract archive only on leak harm; customers rely on the contracts as evidence in disputes. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fine estimates added to the archive's leak ratings
options.B: Availability harm rated with the archive's business owner
options.C: Integrity harm rated with the archive's business owner
options.D: Independent tests of the archive's encryption strength

questions.key_concept: Rate each risk by its harm to confidentiality, integrity and availability; for signed records used as evidence, integrity weighs most, whatever the encryption.
questions.pre_read: Note what customers use the archive for before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption guards against reading the contracts, but the archive's value is that each contract stays exactly as signed; FIPS 199 counts non-repudiation and authenticity under integrity. Since customers use the contracts as evidence, an undetected change is the harm the register misses most. Rating availability harm is the runner-up: an outage delays access, but the contracts survive intact, while an altered contract can lose a customer's dispute.

wrong_explanations.A: Fine estimates refine the leak rating, the one harm already rated; the register stays blind to contracts being changed, the harm that matters most for evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: An outage harms customers too, but it delays access and the contracts survive intact; an altered contract can lose a dispute, so integrity comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing encryption strength checks confidentiality, the one harm already rated; it says nothing about whether a signed contract could be changed unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both stay on confidentiality, the one harm already rated, and neither shows whether a signed contract could be changed unnoticed.
Final two: C beats B because customers use the contracts as evidence; an outage delays access, but an altered contract loses its value.
Exam cue: rate each scenario by confidentiality, integrity and availability, and weigh most the one the business relies on; encryption at rest mainly answers confidentiality.
questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 199 Section 3 (Categorization of Information and Information Systems: impact is rated for confidentiality, integrity and availability, and integrity includes non-repudiation and authenticity); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-01 (the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data-at-rest are protected)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Measuring whether staff report mistakes
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a risk practitioner whether a benefits administrator's staff report their own data-handling mistakes?

options.A: Share of simulated phishing emails that staff report
options.B: Share of staff who say in surveys they would report mistakes
options.C: Count of data-handling mistakes staff report themselves
options.D: Share of filter-flagged misdirected files their senders reported

questions.key_concept: Measure reporting culture by behavior against an independent record: the share of detected mistakes that staff reported themselves, not intent or raw counts.
questions.pre_read: Decide what the measure must show before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Reporting culture shows in what people do after a mistake. Comparing the misdirected member files the email filter flags with those their senders reported gives a share that rises only when more mistakes are reported. A count of self-reported mistakes is the runner-up: it is real behavior, but a fall could mean fewer mistakes or more hidden ones, and the count alone cannot tell which.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting a phishing lure costs staff nothing; owning up to their own mistake is a different behavior, and this measure says nothing about it.
wrong_explanations.B: A survey records what staff say they would do; reporting culture is judged by what they do when a real mistake happens.
wrong_explanations.C: Self-reports are real behavior, but with no record of mistakes to compare against, a falling count could mean fewer mistakes or more hidden ones.

tips: Eliminate: A measures reporting of outside lures and B measures stated intent; neither shows whether staff report the mistakes they actually make.
Final two: D beats C because a share of independently caught mistakes separates reporting from error rates, while a raw count moves with both.
Exam cue: to measure a behavior, compare what people do with an independent record of what happened; surveys and raw counts alone can mislead.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Delivery drones that film each route
questions.question: A drone delivery operator's drones use camera video only to avoid obstacles, but by default upload video of every route, including people in yards, to the cloud. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Uploaded video limited by the data owner to safety staff
options.B: Video processed on board, with none kept or uploaded
options.C: Face blurring before route video is uploaded to the cloud
options.D: A website notice on the filming, approved by the data owner

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design minimizes at the source: data needed only in the moment is processed on the device, not collected or kept.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the video is used for with what the drones send.
questions.correct_explanation: The drones need video only in flight, to see obstacles, so uploading every route collects images of people the purpose never required. Processing the video on board and keeping none removes that collection at its source; the NIST Privacy Framework names processing on local devices as a way to limit observability. Face blurring is the runner-up: it hides faces, but video of homes and yards is still uploaded and kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Limiting access protects the video from misuse, but the operator would still collect and hold footage of people that obstacle avoidance never needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Blurring hides faces, but uploaded video still shows homes and yards at known locations, and the operator keeps footage its purpose never required.
wrong_explanations.D: A notice tells residents about the filming, but it does not reduce what is collected, and people filmed in their yards may never see it.

tips: Eliminate: A restricts who sees the uploads and D announces them, but both leave the operator collecting video of people that obstacle avoidance never needed.
Final two: B beats C because blurring masks faces in video that is still uploaded and kept, while processing on board never collects it.
Exam cue: privacy by design asks first whether data needs to be collected or sent at all; minimizing at the source beats protecting or masking data you never needed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 CT.DP-P1 (data are processed to limit observability and linkability, for example with data actions taking place on local devices); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization)

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). An architecture map older than an acquisition
questions.question: A mortgage servicer's risk analyst is scoping a loan-boarding risk assessment from the enterprise architecture repository, which predates the purchase of two platforms that now board loans. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Confirm loan boarding's current system links with its process owner
options.B: Assess loan boarding from the repository's application map
options.C: Ask the repository's owner to remap the whole enterprise first
options.D: Exclude the two platforms until the repository is updated

questions.key_concept: Enterprise architecture helps only while it is current; before an assessment relies on it, links changed since its last update are confirmed for the scope.
questions.pre_read: Compare the repository's age with what has changed since, before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The repository predates the two platforms that now board loans, so its map misses links the assessment must cover. Confirming loan boarding's current system links with its process owner gives the assessment a sound scope now; NIST PM-7 expects an architecture that is maintained, not drawn once. Remapping the whole enterprise is the runner-up: the repository does need it, but that work is far wider than one assessment and would hold it up.

wrong_explanations.B: The map predates the two platforms that now board loans, so an assessment built on it would miss their links and the risks they bring.
wrong_explanations.C: The repository does need updating, but remapping every system is far wider than this assessment and delays it; the process owner can confirm loan boarding's links now.
wrong_explanations.D: The two platforms now board loans, so leaving them out drops the newest and least understood links from the assessment instead of covering them.

tips: Eliminate: B builds the assessment on a map that misses the two platforms, and D leaves out systems that now board loans; both scope it on outdated architecture.
Final two: A beats C because the assessment needs loan boarding's links now; an enterprise-wide remap fixes the repository but is far wider than this scope.
Exam cue: before an assessment relies on an architecture map, check that it is current for the scope, and confirm changed links with the people who run the process.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. An AI coding agent in the build pipeline
questions.question: A credit bureau's build pipeline lets an AI coding agent write fixes for failed builds, then merge and deploy each fix itself once the automated tests pass. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Weekly review of the agent's merged fixes by the service owner
options.B: More automated tests that each agent fix must pass
options.C: An engineer's approval before each agent fix is merged
options.D: Removal of the agent from the build pipeline

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties in a pipeline covers AI agents: a change an agent writes still needs approval by someone else before it is merged.
questions.pre_read: Trace one fix from the failed build to production before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: When the agent merges its own fixes, the same actor writes and approves each change, so passing tests are the only check. An engineer's approval before each merge restores separation of duties in the pipeline, as for code people write. A weekly review by the service owner is the runner-up: it is a real check, but it comes after the fixes are merged and released, when a faulty or unsafe change may already be running.

wrong_explanations.A: A weekly review finds problems only after the fixes are merged and released, so a faulty or unsafe change can run in production for days first.
wrong_explanations.B: More tests widen what the agent's fixes must pass, but the agent still approves its own changes, and tests check only what they were written to check.
wrong_explanations.D: Removing the agent gives up its benefit when an approval step can control the risk; banning a new tool outright is rarely the proportionate response.

tips: Eliminate: B adds tests yet leaves the agent approving its own changes, and D bans a useful tool when an approval step can control the risk.
Final two: C beats A because approval before merging stops a bad fix reaching production; a weekly review finds it only after it has run.
Exam cue: separation of duties applies to AI agents too; whoever, or whatever, writes a change should not be the one that approves it.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. One wiping method for every retired drive
questions.question: A satellite imagery firm overwrites every retired drive once, whether it held public sample images or restricted defense imagery, and whether it is reissued or sold. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Physical destruction of each retired drive, approved by the data owners
options.B: Methods matched to the data owners' classification and each drive's next use
options.C: A second overwrite pass on each drive the firm sells
options.D: Data owners told of each drive sold and its overwrite result

questions.key_concept: Sanitization is set by the data's classification and where the media goes next, so effort and cost match the harm a disclosure would cause.
questions.pre_read: Picture the different drives this one rule covers before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: One overwrite pass treats restricted defense imagery like public samples, and a sold drive like a reissued one. Setting the method by the data's class and each drive's next use matches effort to risk, as NIST SP 800-88 advises: purge or destroy for restricted imagery leaving the firm, a lighter method for low-risk reuse. Destroying every drive is the runner-up: it protects the imagery, but scraps reusable drives and spends money where risk is low.

wrong_explanations.A: Destruction protects restricted imagery but also scraps drives that held only public images, wasting reusable media and money; the method should match each drive's risk.
wrong_explanations.C: A second pass repeats one method on every sold drive, whatever it held; extra overwrite passes add little, and overwriting can leave data behind on flash drives.
wrong_explanations.D: Telling data owners about each sale reports the problem without fixing it; restricted imagery still leaves the firm after a single overwrite pass.

tips: Eliminate: C repeats a method chosen without regard to the data, and D informs owners while restricted imagery still leaves after one pass.
Final two: B beats A because destroying every drive also scraps ones that held only public images; matching method to class and next use puts effort where risk is.
Exam cue: sanitization depends on how sensitive the data is and whether the media leaves the firm; one method for everything is too weak or too costly.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 4.1 (Storage Sanitization Policy: align the data classification scheme with minimum acceptable sanitization methods, and set requirements for disposal and reuse); NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 4.3 (Storage Sanitization and Disposition Decision Framework: decisions are commensurate with the confidentiality of the information, and purge may suit better than destroy for lease returns, reuse, resale or cost)

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Judging a finished risk-reduction project
questions.question: A fund administrator's portfolio board funded a project to cut payment-fraud risk to a level set in its business case. Which measure BEST shows the risk practitioner whether the project delivered?

options.A: Fraud risk now against the business case's target risk
options.B: Current fraud risk against its rating before the project began
options.C: Delivery against the business case's schedule and budget
options.D: Payment controls now in production against the project plan

questions.key_concept: A risk-reduction project has delivered when residual risk, with its controls working, reaches the target risk its business case promised.
questions.pre_read: Note exactly what the board paid for before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The board funded a cut to a stated level, so the test of delivery is today's residual risk, with the new controls working, against the target risk the business case promised. Comparing current fraud risk with its rating before the project is the runner-up: it shows that risk fell, but not whether it fell as far as the board paid for, so a small drop would look like success.

wrong_explanations.B: A before-and-after comparison shows that fraud risk fell, but not whether it reached the level the board funded; a small drop would still look like success.
wrong_explanations.C: On-time, on-budget delivery shows the project was run well, not that fraud risk reached the level the board paid for.
wrong_explanations.D: Controls in production are outputs; they show what was built, not whether fraud risk now sits at the level the business case promised.

tips: Eliminate: C measures how the project was run and D counts what it built; neither shows whether fraud risk reached the funded level.
Final two: A beats B because the board paid for a stated level; a fall from the old rating can still stop short of it.
Exam cue: judge a risk-reduction investment by residual risk against the target it promised, not by delivery, outputs or any fall at all.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Field controllers with a short patch period
questions.question: A smart-farm operator plans to buy 8,000 wireless valve controllers it expects to run for ten years; the vendor patches their firmware for three years. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A separate network for the controllers after patches stop
options.B: Patch support for the planned life as a purchase term
options.C: Encrypted radio links between the controllers and the farm hub
options.D: Penetration testing of the controllers before they go live

questions.key_concept: For long-lived connected devices, the vendor's patch support should cover the planned years of use; a gap is best closed before purchase.
questions.pre_read: Compare the two time spans in the stem before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The controllers would run seven years after the vendor's patches stop, so flaws found then stay open in devices that steer the farm's water. Making patch support for the planned ten years a purchase term closes that gap at its cause, while the operator still has buying leverage. A separate network is the runner-up: it limits who can reach the controllers, but leaves seven years of flaws unfixed in devices that can still be misused.

wrong_explanations.A: Isolation limits who can reach the controllers, but seven years of flaws would still go unfixed; it suits devices already bought, not a purchase still open.
wrong_explanations.C: Encrypting the radio links protects data in transit, but flaws in the controllers' own firmware would still go unpatched after the third year.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing before go-live finds today's flaws; it cannot fix the ones found after the third year, when no patches will come.

tips: Eliminate: C guards the radio traffic and D finds today's flaws, but the risk lies in firmware flaws found after year three, when no patches come.
Final two: B beats A because a support term closes the gap before purchase; a separate network only limits who can reach controllers left unpatched.
Exam cue: before adopting long-lived devices, compare the vendor's support period with the planned years of use, and close any gap in the purchase terms.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Packages an AI assistant names
questions.question: A robot vacuum maker's firmware developers install packages their AI coding assistant names; one did not exist until an attacker published it with malware. What should the risk practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: Scans of each build's packages for known vulnerabilities
options.B: Code owner review of each code change the AI assistant writes
options.C: The product owner's ban on the AI coding assistant
options.D: Vetting of each new package before it enters the build

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant can name packages attackers then publish, so each new third-party component is vetted before it enters the build.
questions.pre_read: Trace how the malware got into the firmware before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant named a package that did not exist, and an attacker filled that name with malware, so the weak point is how new components enter the build. Vetting each new package before use, against sources the team trusts, stops that at entry, whoever suggested it. Scanning for known vulnerabilities is the runner-up: a useful build check, but a freshly published malicious package has no reported flaw for a scanner to match.

wrong_explanations.A: Known-vulnerability scans match components against reported flaws; a package an attacker has only just published has none on record, so it would pass the scan.
wrong_explanations.B: A code owner sees only the lines that name the package; the malware sits inside the package itself, which this review never opens.
wrong_explanations.C: A ban gives up the assistant's benefit and leaves the gap open: developers can still pull an unvetted or look-alike package from other sources.

tips: Eliminate: B reviews only the code that names the package, not what is inside it, and C bans a useful tool while unvetted packages can still arrive by other routes.
Final two: D beats A because vetting stops an untrusted package at entry; a known-vulnerability scan cannot flag malware nobody has reported yet.
Exam cue: treat an AI suggestion as unverified input; a component, source or fact an AI names is checked like any other before it is used.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Auction data and its RPO
questions.question: A fish auction's records owner set a one-hour RPO, as lost sale records leave catches unbilled; IT backs the auction database up nightly to another region. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Backups of the auction database at least hourly
options.B: Restore tests of the backups held in the other region
options.C: An offline copy of each nightly auction backup
options.D: The records owner's review of the one-hour RPO

questions.key_concept: Backup frequency must meet the RPO the business set; when backups miss it, change the backup design, not a target set on real harm.
questions.pre_read: Work out how much auction data could be lost today, then read the options.
questions.correct_explanation: With nightly backups, a failure just before the next backup could lose a whole day of sales, far beyond the one-hour RPO the owner set because lost records leave catches unbilled. Backing up at least hourly brings the loss window inside the RPO, the basis CP-9 gives for backup frequency. The owner's review of the RPO is the runner-up: owners can revisit targets, but this one rests on stated harm, so the design must change.

wrong_explanations.B: Restore tests show the copies can be recovered, which is worth knowing, but a perfect restore still brings back data up to a day old.
wrong_explanations.C: An offline copy guards backups against ransomware and site loss, but it holds the same nightly data, so the loss window stays near a day.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner set the RPO from the harm of unbilled catches; asking them to loosen it bends a business need to fit IT's schedule.

tips: Eliminate: B proves the copies restore and C adds a safer copy, but both still bring back data up to a day old.
Final two: A beats D because the RPO rests on harm the owner has already weighed; when backups miss it, the design changes, not the target.
Exam cue: RPO sets how often data is copied and RTO how fast it comes back; close a data-loss gap with copy frequency, not restore tests or extra copies.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Docks cut off from the server
questions.question: A bike-share operator's docks release bikes freely when offline from its server; the risk analyst has costed theft under this setting and stranded-rider fines under a locked one. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Set the docks to stay locked when cut off from the server
options.B: Have the risk owner choose the docks' failure setting
options.C: Have senior management choose the docks' failure setting
options.D: Fit GPS trackers to bikes taken while docks are offline

questions.key_concept: Failing open or failing secure trades availability against protection; once both costs are analyzed, the risk owner chooses the failure setting.
questions.pre_read: Note what has already been done and what is still undecided before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Releasing bikes offline keeps the service available to riders; locking them protects the fleet. SC-24 ties the choice of failure state to mission and business needs, and the analyst has already costed both sides, so the decision now belongs to the risk owner. Locked docks are the runner-up: a secure default feels safe, but it swaps theft for stranded-rider fines, and recommending it would make the owner's trade-off for them.

wrong_explanations.A: Failing locked is not automatically safer: it swaps theft losses for stranded-rider fines, and weighing those two costs is a business decision, not a security default.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management, with the board, sets appetite and oversees risk, but choosing one service's failure setting within that appetite belongs to the service's risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Trackers may recover some bikes, but they settle neither side of the trade-off; anyone could still take a bike during each outage.

tips: Eliminate: C hands one service's setting to senior management, beyond its role, and D adds trackers that recover bikes without settling the open-or-locked choice.
Final two: B beats A because both settings carry a business cost the analyst has priced; recommending locked docks would make the owner's trade-off for them.
Exam cue: fail open or fail secure trades availability against protection; once both costs are known, the risk owner chooses, not the security default.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Phishing clicks at five clinics
questions.question: A rural clinic network's yearly security course is a video in English; at five clinics where most staff speak little English, phishing clicks run triple the average. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: The English course repeated until the staff pass its quiz
options.B: Stricter email filtering for the five clinics
options.C: Warnings for staff who click on phishing emails
options.D: Awareness training in the staff's own language

questions.key_concept: Awareness changes behavior only when the audience can follow it, so content and delivery fit each group's language and work setting.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the course works at most clinics but not at these five.
questions.correct_explanation: The course reaches the five clinics, but most staff there cannot follow it, so it never changes how they handle email; that is the cause behind the triple click rate. Training in their own language fixes the cause, as SP 800-50 asks that material fit the learners' needs. Stricter email filtering is the runner-up: a sound extra layer, but some phishing always gets through, and these staff would meet it still untrained.

wrong_explanations.A: Repeating a course staff cannot follow adds hours, not understanding; passing a quiz on the third try does not show changed behavior.
wrong_explanations.B: Filtering cuts how much phishing arrives, but none is complete; staff who receive what gets through would still have had no training they could follow.
wrong_explanations.C: Warnings blame staff for a gap in the program; people never taught in a language they follow need teaching, not penalties.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a course staff cannot follow, and C blames staff for a program that never reached them.
Final two: D beats B because the cause is training staff cannot follow; filtering adds a layer but leaves them untrained for what gets through.
Exam cue: when awareness fails in one group, ask whether that group could follow it; fit language and format to the audience before adding volume or penalties.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Putting an old register online
questions.question: A national archive plans to put a scanned 1970s school register online, with pupils' names, birth dates and disciplinary notes; most pupils are likely still alive. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Online access limited to registered archive readers
options.B: The collection owner's approval to publish with a takedown route
options.C: The collection owner's release with entries on living people withheld
options.D: A page notice that the register is a historical record

questions.key_concept: Old records hold personal data at least while the people in them live; release withholds what could harm them rather than awaiting takedown requests.
questions.pre_read: Picture one pupil named in the register today before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The register links names and birth dates to disciplinary notes about people mostly still alive, so putting it online could harm them. Withholding living pupils' entries until release can no longer harm them protects those people; the collection owner decides, as data owner. Publishing with a takedown route is the runner-up: it helps, but the harm happens when the notes first appear, and most pupils would never know to ask.

wrong_explanations.A: Reader registration narrows who can open the register, but many readers could still see living people's disciplinary notes; privacy turns on what is disclosed, not only to whom.
wrong_explanations.B: A takedown route acts only after a pupil finds their entry and asks; by then the notes have been seen and copied, and most will never know to look.
wrong_explanations.D: A notice explains what the register is but does not change what it reveals; living pupils' disciplinary notes would be exposed all the same.

tips: Eliminate: A only narrows who can open the register and D labels it, but both still expose living pupils' disciplinary notes.
Final two: C beats B because withholding prevents the harm before release; a takedown route acts only after the notes have been seen.
Exam cue: for personal data in published or shared records, prefer limiting what is disclosed up front over reacting to complaints after release.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Old and new systems side by side
questions.question: An auto parts supplier's ERP move runs old and new systems side by side, passing orders between them, but its architecture review covered only the finished design. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A risk assessment of each interim stage of the move
options.B: Reconciliation of the orders passed between the two systems
options.C: The order process owner's approval of the finished design
options.D: A post-implementation assessment once the new ERP is fully live

questions.key_concept: A phased move creates interim states, with old and new systems linked, whose risks a review of the finished design does not cover.
questions.pre_read: Note what the review looked at, and when each part of the move happens.
questions.correct_explanation: Running old and new systems side by side, with orders passing between them, adds links and complexity that exist only during the move; a review of the finished design never saw them. Assessing each interim stage finds those risks so controls can be chosen. Reconciling orders between the systems is the runner-up: a sound control for one likely risk, but it is chosen before the interim risks are analyzed and may miss others.

wrong_explanations.B: Reconciliation catches orders lost or altered between the systems, one interim risk; chosen before the interim stages are assessed, it may leave others, such as extra access paths, untreated.
wrong_explanations.C: The finished design was already reviewed; the owner approving it says nothing about the months when old and new systems run together and exchange orders.
wrong_explanations.D: An assessment after go-live comes once the interim stages are over, so whatever risk they carried would already have been borne, not managed.

tips: Eliminate: C approves a finished design that was already reviewed, and D assesses only after the interim stages have passed.
Final two: A beats B because the interim risks are not yet analyzed; reconciliation treats one of them before anyone knows what the rest are.
Exam cue: when a change runs in stages, the in-between states carry their own risk; assess those, not only the end state, before choosing controls.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. A security patch during a change freeze
questions.question: During an online marketplace's peak-season change freeze, its payment software vendor releases a patch for a flaw that attackers are actively exploiting. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Install the patch now and log the change after the freeze
options.B: Keep the freeze and install the patch once it ends
options.C: Route the patch through the emergency change process
options.D: Have the platform owner waive testing to install it sooner

questions.key_concept: A change freeze does not stop urgent fixes; they go through the emergency change route, with fast approval, testing and a back-out plan.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the freeze protects against what the flaw threatens before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: An actively exploited flaw in payment software is hard to leave open through peak season, yet the freeze exists to stop unplanned breakage. The emergency change process serves both: fast, authorized approval, testing in proportion to the urgency, a back-out plan and a review afterward. Installing now and logging later is the runner-up: it is quick, but skips approval, testing and back-out, so a faulty install could stop payments at the busiest time.

wrong_explanations.A: Logging afterward keeps a record but skips the approval, testing and back-out plan that make an urgent change safe; a faulty install could halt payments at peak.
wrong_explanations.B: Holding the patch leaves an actively exploited flaw open in payment software through the busiest period; a freeze channels urgent fixes through a controlled route rather than blocking them.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing is what keeps an urgent patch from breaking payments; the platform owner waiving it swaps one risk for another, outside the emergency approval route.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves an exploited flaw open through peak season, and D drops the testing that keeps an urgent patch from breaking payments.
Final two: C beats A because the emergency route keeps approval, testing and back-out at speed; logging after the fact keeps only the record.
Exam cue: urgency changes the change path, not the need for control; look for the emergency process rather than a bypass or a delay.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Matter files for a fine-tuned assistant
questions.question: A law firm will fine-tune a drafting assistant on all closed matter files for use by every lawyer; most files are visible only to their matter team. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data owners reclassify the matter files for firm-wide use
options.B: Exclude restricted matter files from the training set
options.C: Add output filters that strip client names from drafts
options.D: Have the system owner encrypt the training set at rest

questions.key_concept: Access rules do not carry into a trained model, which can repeat what it learned; train only on data all its users may see.
questions.pre_read: Compare who may open each file today with who will use the assistant.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning folds every file into the model, and a model can repeat what it learned (data memorization); the per-matter access rules on the files do not come with it. Excluding restricted matter files keeps what the assistant can repeat within what every lawyer may already see. Output filters stripping client names are the runner-up: they catch one identifier, but facts, strategy and terms from restricted matters could still surface in drafts.

wrong_explanations.A: Classification follows the files' sensitivity and the firm's duty to each client, not a tool's needs; relabeling them would open restricted matters to every lawyer.
wrong_explanations.C: Filters catch the identifiers they are told to look for; a draft can still reveal a restricted matter's facts or strategy with no client name in it.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption at rest protects the stored training set from theft, but the model has already learned its content and can repeat it to any user.

tips: Eliminate: A relabels restricted files to suit the tool, and D protects the stored copy while the model still holds what it learned.
Final two: B beats C because it keeps restricted content out of the model; filters screen only some of what the model might repeat.
Exam cue: access rules stay with the files, not with a model trained on them; match what goes into training to who will use the model.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. A vendor building for a fixed price
questions.question: A vendor is building a regional hospital's patient portal for a fixed price, reporting only dates and budget; the hospital keeps no risk log for the project. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the fixed price to cap the hospital's exposure
options.B: Ask internal audit to review the vendor's project risks
options.C: Add a late-delivery penalty to the vendor's contract
options.D: Have the portal's owner review project risks with the vendor

questions.key_concept: A fixed price moves overrun costs to the vendor, not the hospital's accountability for the portal's risks, which its business owner keeps tracking.
questions.pre_read: List what the vendor's reports cover and what they leave out.
questions.correct_explanation: A fixed price moves overrun costs to the vendor, yet the hospital still answers for a portal that will hold patient data, and the vendor's reports say nothing on security, privacy or quality. Having the portal's business owner review project risks with the vendor gives the hospital that view. A late-delivery penalty is the runner-up: it adds leverage on dates, but prices one risk and may push the vendor to cut testing.

wrong_explanations.A: A fixed price caps what the hospital pays, not what it could lose; a breach of patient data or a faulty portal would still land on the hospital.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; asking it to review the vendor's project risks does not give the portal's owner a running view of the project's risks.
wrong_explanations.C: A penalty compensates for lateness, one risk among many, and can push the vendor to trim testing to hit the date; it shows nothing of the other risks.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a cap on cost as a cap on the hospital's loss, and B hands the project's risk view to assurance rather than to its owner.
Final two: D beats C because a penalty only prices lateness; the portal's owner still needs to see and act on the project's other risks.
Exam cue: contracts and penalties move cost, not accountability; the business owner keeps tracking the risks of work a vendor delivers.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. A rejected data source on new terms
questions.question: In 2023 a national statistics office's leaders turned down phone location data for commuting statistics, as no telecom would supply it aggregated; one telecom now offers aggregated counts. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the data's risks and benefits as now offered
options.B: Have the commuting statistics owner approve the data's use
options.C: Keep the rejection the leaders reached in 2023
options.D: Take the telecom's word that the counts cannot identify anyone

questions.key_concept: When the facts behind an emerging-technology decision change, the risks and benefits are reassessed before the earlier ban stands or a new approval is given.
questions.pre_read: Note what has changed since the 2023 decision before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The 2023 rejection rested on one fact, that no telecom would aggregate the data, and that fact has changed. A fresh assessment weighs the new offer's threats, such as re-identification from small counts or reliance on one supplier, against its benefits for commuting statistics. Owner approval is the runner-up: a business decision does follow, but approving now would come before anyone has analyzed the data as now offered.

wrong_explanations.B: Approval is a business decision that follows analysis; approving now would take on the new offer's risks before anyone has assessed them.
wrong_explanations.C: The 2023 rejection rested on a fact that has changed; keeping it without a fresh look could forgo real value for a reason that no longer holds.
wrong_explanations.D: A supplier's statement is a claim, not evidence; whether small counts could identify people needs checking against how the counts are built.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a decision whose reason no longer holds, and D takes a supplier's claim in place of evidence.
Final two: A beats B because the business decision comes after analysis; approving now skips the risks of the data as offered today.
Exam cue: when the facts behind a past yes or no change, reassess before keeping the old decision or making a new one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task P-14 (Risk Assessment for the System: conduct a system-level risk assessment from initiation and update it on an ongoing basis); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-07 (strategic opportunities or positive risks are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions)

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). One password across every unit
questions.question: A medical device maker's infusion pump design gives every unit the same administrator password, and the draft manual tells hospitals to change it at setup. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A longer shared pump password chosen by the product owner
options.B: Training for hospital staff on changing it at setup
options.C: A risk owner's contract term making hospitals liable
options.D: A unique password set on each pump at the factory

questions.key_concept: Secure settings belong in the design by default; relying on each customer to change a shared default password leaves units exposed.
questions.pre_read: Note who must act for the design to be safe, and what happens when one of them does not.
questions.correct_explanation: One password shared by every pump means a single leak exposes every unit whose hospital skipped the change, and the design relies on each customer to act. Setting a unique password on each pump at the factory removes the shared secret at the source. Training hospital staff is the runner-up: it raises how many hospitals change the password, but any that miss the step still leave pumps open to anyone who knows it.

wrong_explanations.A: A longer password is harder to guess but is still one secret shared by every pump; once it leaks or is published, every unchanged unit is open.
wrong_explanations.B: Training helps more hospitals make the change, but security that depends on every customer acting leaves pumps exposed wherever one step is missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Shifting liability to hospitals moves cost, not the hazard; patients are still at risk from pumps that anyone with the shared password can reach.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps one secret shared across every pump, and C shifts liability while the hazard to patients stays.
Final two: D beats B because a unique factory password removes the shared secret by design; training still relies on each hospital acting.
Exam cue: when a design leaves a security step to every customer, prefer the option that makes the default secure before the product ships.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 PW.9 (Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default: reduce the likelihood of software being deployed with weak security settings); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management: default authenticators are changed before first use, as factory default credentials are often well known and a significant risk)

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Tests of a standby ground station
questions.question: A satellite operator's switchover tests always end once its standby ground station has control; the plan says control returns to the main station within 10 days. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a second standby ground station far from the main one
options.B: Have the plan owner test the hand-back to the main station
options.C: Have the plan owner measure each switchover against the RTO
options.D: Double the number of switchover tests the plan requires

questions.key_concept: Recovery tests cover the whole cycle, including the return to the main site, because an untested hand-back can cause a second outage.
questions.pre_read: List the steps the plan relies on, then check which of them the tests actually run.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan relies on handing control back to the main station within 10 days, yet no test has ever done it, so that step is an untested assumption; a failed hand-back could cut control again or lose records made at the standby. Measuring each switchover against the RTO is the runner-up: it adds detail on a step tests already prove and leaves the hand-back unproven.

wrong_explanations.A: A second standby adds capacity, but control would still have to come back to the main station by a step no test has run.
wrong_explanations.C: Tests already prove the switchover; measuring it against the RTO adds detail there and leaves the hand-back the plan relies on unproven.
wrong_explanations.D: More switchovers repeat the step tests already prove; how often a test runs matters less than whether it covers every step of recovery.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a standby that would face the same untested hand-back, and D runs more tests of a step the tests already prove.
Final two: B beats C because the plan relies on the hand-back within 10 days, and only B puts that untested step under test.
Exam cue: a recovery test proves only the steps it runs; check tests against every step the plan relies on, including the return to normal.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. An AI agent calling a payments service
questions.question: A home insurer's new AI claims agent will call its payments service, which accepts any request from inside the data center network. Which control should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: The claims owner's sign-off on the AI agent before it goes live
options.B: A separate network segment just for the claims agent's servers
options.C: A check of the agent's identity and rights on each call
options.D: Encryption of traffic between the agent and the service

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust gives network location no trust: a service authenticates and authorizes every caller, AI agents included, per session or request.
questions.pre_read: Note what the payments service trusts today, then ask which option changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust grants nothing for network location: each request is checked for who is calling and what that caller may do. Checking the agent's own identity and rights on every call stops payments being accepted just because they come from inside, and limits what a misused agent can do. A separate segment is the runner-up: it narrows which systems can connect, but the service would still trust whatever reaches it.

wrong_explanations.A: A sign-off before launch is a one-time approval; once live, the payments service would still accept any request from inside, from the agent or anything else.
wrong_explanations.B: A segment limits which systems can connect, but the payments service would still trust whatever reaches it, including a misused or impersonated agent.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption keeps traffic private and unaltered in transit; it does not tell the payments service whether the caller may request a payment.

tips: Eliminate: A approves the agent once with nothing checked when it runs, and D protects traffic in transit without deciding who may call.
Final two: C beats B because Zero Trust checks every request's identity and rights; a segment still trusts whatever reaches the service.
Exam cue: under Zero Trust, ask what is checked on each request; a control that trusts where a call comes from falls short, for AI agents too.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust: network location alone does not imply trust, and access to each enterprise resource is granted per session); NIST SP 800-207 Section 5.7 (Use of Non-person Entities in ZTA Administration: software agents, AI included, are assumed to authenticate when calling resources, and an attacker may induce an agent to perform tasks the attacker is not privileged to perform)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. New risk owners after a restructuring
questions.question: Since a restructuring, a cosmetics brand's new risk owners send every accept-or-treat decision to the risk team, believing the decisions are its job; 14 are overdue. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Train the risk owners on the decisions their role holds
options.B: Escalate the 14 overdue decisions to the executive committee
options.C: Take the decisions into the risk team during the transition
options.D: Add automatic reminders for overdue decisions in the register

questions.key_concept: Role-based training gives people with risk duties, such as newly appointed risk owners, what they need to make the decisions their role holds.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask what it would change and what it would leave as it is.
questions.correct_explanation: The new owners believe these decisions belong to the risk team, so the cause is a misunderstanding of their role: role-based training shows each owner which accept-or-treat decisions are theirs, with the risk team advising. Escalating the overdue decisions is the runner-up: it clears today's backlog by moving the decisions to executives, but the owners would keep sending new ones to the risk team.

wrong_explanations.B: Escalation moves today's 14 decisions to executives, who do not own these risks, and leaves the cause in place, so new decisions keep coming back.
wrong_explanations.C: Accept-or-treat decisions belong to the risk owners; the risk team advises, and deciding for them, even for a while, takes on accountability it cannot hold.
wrong_explanations.D: Reminders tell owners a decision is late, but these owners send decisions on because they think the risk team decides, so a reminder changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C has the risk team take decisions that belong to the owners, and D reminds owners who are not forgetting but misreading their role.
Final two: A beats B because training fixes why the decisions reach the risk team; escalating clears the backlog but leaves the owners misreading their role.
Exam cue: when people new to a risk role keep handing their decisions back, teach the role before escalating or deciding for them.
