questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Ad tracking on tax-filing pages
questions.question: A tax agency's communications team put an ad platform's tracking code on its online filing pages to measure a campaign; the platform may reuse what it collects. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: List the tracking code in the site's privacy notice
options.B: Get the campaign owner to approve the platform's terms
options.C: Scan the filing pages for security flaws the tracking code adds
options.D: Move the tracking code to pages that hold no taxpayer data

questions.key_concept: Third-party tracking code can pass what a page shows to its owner, so keep it off pages holding personal data such as tax filings.
questions.pre_read: Work out what the tracking code can see on each page and who receives it.
questions.correct_explanation: Filing pages hold taxpayer data collected to administer tax, and code on them can pass what a page shows to the platform, which may reuse it for its own ends. Moving the code to pages with no taxpayer data stops that disclosure and still measures the campaign. Listing the code in the privacy notice is the runner-up: taxpayers would be told, but their data would still go beyond the purpose it was collected for.

wrong_explanations.A: A notice tells taxpayers about the disclosure; it does not make sending filing data to an ad platform for its own reuse fit the purpose of collection.
wrong_explanations.B: The campaign owner runs the campaign, not the taxpayer data; disclosure is the data owner's call, and approved terms would still let the platform reuse it.
wrong_explanations.C: A security scan looks for weaknesses the code brings, but the privacy problem is the code working as designed and sending page data to the platform.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the campaign's owner approve disclosing data that is not theirs, and C looks for security flaws while the code works as designed.
Final two: D beats A because it stops taxpayer data reaching the platform; a notice describes the disclosure but leaves it outside the filing purpose.
Exam cue: privacy asks whether data should reach a party at all; telling people or securing the flow does not cure a disclosure beyond the purpose.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Test data for a vendor's AI tool
questions.question: To test a vendor's AI tool for spotting duplicate voter registrations, an election commission offers a roll copy with names randomized but birth dates and addresses intact. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: The roll copy with its birth dates and addresses masked as well
options.B: The full roll, shared under the data owner's signed agreement
options.C: Synthetic registrations that include a few pairs known to match
options.D: The offered copy, deleted by the vendor once testing ends

questions.key_concept: Test data for an AI tool must protect the people behind it and still prove something; synthetic records with known answers do both.
questions.pre_read: For each test data option, ask what it exposes and what the test could still measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Birth dates and addresses still identify voters, and randomized names break the matches the tool must find, so the offered copy both exposes people and weakens the test. Synthetic registrations with planted duplicate pairs, including realistic spelling variants, expose no voter and give known answers to measure what the tool catches and misses. Masking birth dates and addresses too is the runner-up: it protects voters but erases the near-matches the test needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Masking every identifying field protects voters, but it erases the spelling variants and near-matches the tool must find, so the test cannot show how well it works.
wrong_explanations.B: An agreement and the data owner's signature limit what the vendor may do, but every voter's real record still leaves the commission for a test that needs none.
wrong_explanations.D: Deleting the copy afterward limits how long the vendor holds it, but birth dates and addresses still identify voters throughout the test, and random names still weaken it.

tips: Eliminate: B sends every voter's real record to the vendor for a test that needs none, and D leaves birth dates and addresses that identify voters during the test.
Final two: C beats A because planted duplicates give the test known answers to find; masking every field protects voters but erases the near-matches the tool must find.
Exam cue: good test data does two jobs, protecting the people behind it and letting the test prove something; choose the option that does both.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. A recurring pre-approved change
questions.question: A public transit authority's monthly fare-table load is a pre-approved standard change; this month's load meets every criterion, and nothing has failed or changed since approval. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send this standard change to the change board for full review
options.B: Keep the load's standard route until its next scheduled review
options.C: Get the fare system owner to approve this load before it runs
options.D: Reclassify fare loads as normal changes, agreed with the system owner

questions.key_concept: A standard change that meets its criteria, with nothing failed or changed since approval, runs on its routine path until its scheduled review.
questions.pre_read: Before reading the options, list what has changed since this type of change was approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard changes are pre-approved because they are low risk and proven; each run is still tested and recorded but skips fresh review, so effort goes where risk is. This load meets every criterion, and nothing has failed or changed, so no trigger calls for more; the next scheduled review checks the type still qualifies. Owner approval before the run is the runner-up: it looks careful but re-decides what the pre-approval settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Full board review suits changes whose risk is unknown or high; sending a proven, pre-approved change there spends the board's time on low risk it has already judged.
wrong_explanations.C: An extra approval before the run looks careful, but pre-approval already settled this type of change, and nothing has failed or changed to reopen that decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Withdrawing standard status fits a change type that has failed or whose system has changed; with neither, it moves proven, low-risk work back to full review.

tips: Eliminate: A sends a proven standard change to the board, and D withdraws its standard status, yet nothing has failed or changed to call for either.
Final two: B beats C because the pre-approval already covers this run; with no trigger, the next scheduled review, not a fresh approval, is the check.
Exam cue: a pre-approved change that meets its criteria with no trigger keeps its routine path; extra review is for changes that fail, change or fall outside.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Timing a legacy replacement
questions.question: A customs broker's IT team will replace its unsupported declaration system after the import peak; the risk practitioner has rated replacing it before and after the peak. What should the practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the declaration process owner choose the replacement timing
options.B: Keep IT's plan to replace the system after the import peak ends
options.C: Scan the unsupported system for new flaws until the replacement is live
options.D: Move the replacement to before the peak to end the legacy exposure

questions.key_concept: When a legacy system's replacement timing trades one rated risk against another, the business owner of the process chooses; IT and the practitioner inform.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risk each timing carries, and whose objectives bear it.
questions.correct_explanation: Each timing carries a rated risk: replacing after the peak keeps the unsupported system in use through the busiest period, while replacing before it risks a new system failing as volumes rise. Choosing between them is a business risk decision, so the declaration process owner makes it on both ratings. Keeping IT's plan is the runner-up: it may prove the better date, but IT would be settling a business trade-off the owner has not seen.

wrong_explanations.B: IT's date may turn out right, but it settles which risk the business carries through the peak, a decision for the declaration process owner, not IT.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning finds flaws the vendor will no longer fix, so it lowers no risk on its own, and it leaves the timing choice unmade.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the date ends the legacy exposure sooner but takes on the rated risk of a cut-over close to the peak; that trade-off is the owner's to make.

tips: Eliminate: C only scans a system its vendor no longer patches, which leaves the timing unchosen, and D swaps one rated risk for the other without the owner.
Final two: A beats B because the timing decides which risk the business carries through its peak; IT's plan may be sound, but the owner decides.
Exam cue: when two options trade one rated risk for another, look for the business owner choosing with the ratings, not IT or the practitioner.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Ordering security stories in a backlog
questions.question: A smart-meter installer's product owner orders the backlog within limits the risk owner set; two security stories, both rated inside those limits, compete for one sprint slot. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Refer the choice between the two stories back to the risk owner
options.B: Add both stories to the sprint, moving planned features out
options.C: Leave the choice between the two stories to the product owner
options.D: Rank the two stories for the team by their risk scores

questions.key_concept: Within the risk owner's limits, the product owner orders the backlog; only choices that would breach them go back to the risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing, note which decisions the stem says have already been made, and by whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk owner has already set the limits and left backlog order inside them to the product owner, who weighs security work against features. Both stories sit within those limits, so either order keeps risk acceptable, and the choice is the product owner's. Referring it to the risk owner is the runner-up: it looks cautious, but it sends back a decision the owner delegated; escalation is for choices that would breach the limits.

wrong_explanations.A: Referral fits a choice that would breach the risk owner's limits; both stories sit inside them, so this sends back a decision already delegated to the product owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Taking both stories pushes out features the product owner planned, though neither story's risk calls for it; within the limits, that trade-off is the product owner's.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk scores inform the choice, but ranking the stories for the team makes the practitioner the decider of a backlog order that belongs to the product owner.

tips: Eliminate: D has the practitioner order the backlog, and B takes both stories, pushing out planned features, when neither story's risk calls for it.
Final two: C beats A because both stories sit inside limits the risk owner already set; referral is for choices that would breach them.
Exam cue: delegation inside limits is a decision already made; send a choice upward only when it would break those limits.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. A virtual power plant platform
questions.question: A solar installer's leaders want to join a virtual power plant platform, which would control customers' home batteries, because three rivals have joined. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Evaluate the threats from the platform's control of customers' home batteries
options.B: Set out what business result the installer needs the platform to achieve
options.C: Plan the platform's rollout with the field operations owner
options.D: Join the platform now to keep pace with the three rival installers

questions.key_concept: Before weighing a new technology's threats and opportunities, establish which business objective it would serve; following rivals is not an objective.
questions.pre_read: Order the options by what each depends on, then pick the one nothing else can skip.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is judged against objectives, so a technology can be weighed only against the business result the installer needs from it, such as new revenue or savings for customers. Here the only reason given is that rivals joined. Setting out the objective comes first; it frames which threats and opportunities matter. Evaluating the battery-control threats is the runner-up: it is needed, but without the objective there is no benefit to weigh them against.

wrong_explanations.A: Remote battery control is a real threat to assess, but without a stated objective there is no benefit to weigh it against, so the assessment cannot reach a decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Planning the rollout with the field operations owner treats joining as decided, before anyone has set the objective or weighed the platform's risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Joining because rivals did is adopting without analysis; their reasons and exposures may differ from the installer's, and nothing yet shows what joining would achieve.

tips: Eliminate: D adopts because rivals did, and C plans the rollout with an owner before anyone has decided to join or weighed the risks.
Final two: B beats A because threats can be weighed only against what the installer needs the platform to achieve; set that out first.
Exam cue: when the only reason for a new technology is that others use it, the FIRST step is to name the business objective it would serve.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). AI forecasting outside the target architecture
questions.question: A power trading firm's desk sends live positions to an AI forecasting service it added outside the target architecture; the service trains one model on all clients' inputs. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Fees for the service paid outside the approved IT budget
options.B: A service that breaks the firm's architecture standards
options.C: Bids resting on forecasts from a model the firm cannot inspect
options.D: Live positions shaping forecasts that other clients receive

questions.key_concept: An AI service added outside the target architecture can skip its data rules; one that trains on inputs lets confidential data shape other clients' results.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states as fact from risks it never mentions, then weigh the stated ones by business harm.
questions.correct_explanation: The service trains one model on all clients' inputs, so the desk's live positions become training data that shapes forecasts for other clients, possibly rivals, and is hard to pull back. Adding it outside the architecture skipped the review that would catch that term. A model the firm cannot inspect is the runner-up: a fair concern with any outside model, but the stem shows no faulty forecasts, and the desk can test them.

wrong_explanations.A: Spending outside the IT budget is a governance lapse to correct, but it exposes no trading data; the exposure lies in where the positions go.
wrong_explanations.B: A departure from the architecture matters mostly for what it exposes; here the exposure is the positions the service trains on.
wrong_explanations.C: Opacity is a fair concern with any vendor model, but the stem shows no faulty forecasts, and testing can check them; the training term exposes positions now.

tips: Eliminate: A is a budget lapse, not an exposure, and B treats the departure from the architecture as the harm; a deviation matters for what it exposes.
Final two: D beats C because the stem says the service trains on all clients' inputs, so the positions are exposed now; poor forecasts are possible but unshown and testable.
Exam cue: for technology added outside the architecture, look past the deviation itself to the business exposure the stem's facts make certain.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Skipping a post-implementation review
questions.question: A smart-lock maker's product owner wants to skip the remote-unlock app's post-implementation review, as no incidents occurred in three months; its risk rating assumes the designed controls work. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the product owner to hold the review as planned
options.B: Lower the app's risk rating on its clean incident record
options.C: Commission a penetration test of the live app
options.D: Close the project on the product owner's sign-off

questions.key_concept: Quiet early months do not show a new system's controls work; the post-implementation review checks the controls its risk rating relies on.
questions.pre_read: Note what the risk rating rests on, then ask what evidence each option would produce about it.
questions.correct_explanation: The app's rating assumes its designed controls are in place and working. Three months without incidents does little to show that: a missing control may simply not have been tested by an attacker yet. The post-implementation review checks the designed controls, technical and procedural, and whether risks stayed within appetite. A penetration test is the runner-up: useful evidence, but it probes for exploitable flaws in part of the app and leaves other assumed controls unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Three quiet months is weak evidence, and lowering the rating credits controls no one has checked; the review would supply that evidence first.
wrong_explanations.C: A penetration test probes part of the app for exploitable flaws; it leaves procedural and other designed controls the rating assumes unconfirmed.
wrong_explanations.D: Closing on the product owner's sign-off skips the check that the controls work; a sign-off records a decision, not evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B credits controls on an absence of incidents, and D closes the project on a sign-off; neither checks that the designed controls exist and work.
Final two: A beats C because the review checks the designed controls the rating assumes; a penetration test probes for exploitable flaws in part of the app.
Exam cue: no incidents is not evidence that controls work; after go-live, confirm the controls a rating relies on before crediting them.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. A retest after another service's outage
questions.question: A fire service tests dispatch failover yearly and after hosting or RTO changes; neither changed, and a neighbor's outage came from software the service does not use. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Run an extra failover test agreed with the dispatch owner
options.B: Add outages at other services to the retest triggers
options.C: Shorten the dispatch RTO, agreed with the dispatch owner
options.D: Have IT operations run the next scheduled failover test

questions.key_concept: An incident elsewhere prompts a recovery retest when it shares a cause with your setup; one sharing none leaves the test schedule as it is.
questions.pre_read: List the test's stated triggers, then check whether any fact in the stem meets one.
questions.correct_explanation: The service retests dispatch failover yearly and after hosting or RTO changes. Neither changed, and the neighbor's outage came from software this service does not use, so no trigger is met and the next scheduled test, run by IT operations, the team that performs the technical failover, is the right point. An extra test agreed with the dispatch owner is the runner-up: the owner may accept its disruption, but it retests unchanged conditions.

wrong_explanations.A: The dispatch owner could accept the disruption, but no trigger is met, so an extra test re-proves unchanged conditions, adding effort and disruption for no new finding.
wrong_explanations.B: Outages elsewhere matter when they share a cause with this service; a trigger for every outside outage would retest after events, like this one, that share none.
wrong_explanations.C: The RTO comes from the business impact of losing dispatch, which the neighbor's outage does not change; shortening it answers a risk this service does not face.

tips: Eliminate: B makes outages elsewhere a retest trigger, and C shortens an RTO set by business impact; the neighbor's outage changes neither for this service.
Final two: D beats A because none of the stated triggers is met; an extra test, even with the owner's consent, retests unchanged conditions.
Exam cue: before retesting after an outage elsewhere, ask whether its cause applies to your own setup; if not, and no trigger is met, keep the schedule.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Access reviews under per-session checks
questions.question: A data-center cooling contractor checks technicians' identity and device in each remote session to clients' chillers; its IT director proposes ending access-rights reviews. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Drop the access-rights reviews as the IT director proposes
options.B: Add a second sign-in factor for every technician
options.C: Keep reviewing which clients each technician can reach
options.D: Replace the reviews with alerts on unusual sessions

questions.key_concept: Per-session checks enforce whatever rights the policy grants; reviews still find rights a person no longer needs, such as a former client's systems.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each control actually checks, and which kind of failure each one would miss.
questions.correct_explanation: Checking identity and device in each session confirms who is connecting, then grants whatever rights the policy holds. It cannot tell that a technician moved off a client's account should no longer reach that client's chillers; reviews of access rights find those stale grants. Alerts on unusual sessions are the runner-up: they catch odd behavior, but a technician using rights they should have lost works normally and raises no alert.

wrong_explanations.A: Dropping the reviews treats session checks as judging rights they only enforce; stale grants then stay usable with no one looking for them.
wrong_explanations.B: A second factor strengthens proof of identity, which the session checks already cover; the gap is rights no one has re-checked.
wrong_explanations.D: Alerts catch unusual sessions, but use of a stale yet granted right looks normal, so it raises no alert and the grant stays.

tips: Eliminate: A treats per-session checks as reviewing rights they only enforce, and B adds identity proof the sessions already check; neither finds rights no longer needed.
Final two: C beats D because a stale grant used normally raises no alert; a review of rights asks whether each grant is still needed.
Exam cue: access checks enforce the rights granted but do not judge them; a review must still ask whether each grant is needed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 5.3 (Stolen Credentials/Insider Threat: Zero Trust stops compromised accounts or assets from moving laterally, but a valid account can still reach the resources it is granted); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges: review assigned privileges to validate the need for them, and reassign or remove them if necessary)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Starting phishing simulations
questions.question: A vehicle inspection center's IT manager plans its first phishing simulations without telling staff a program exists, so click rates stay honest. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Explain the program to process owners but not staff
options.B: Announce the program to staff without naming test dates
options.C: Announce the date of each simulation to staff beforehand
options.D: Hold one unannounced baseline round before giving any notice

questions.key_concept: Phishing simulations are announced as a program but not by date: random timing keeps results honest while staff know the tests exist to teach.
questions.pre_read: Decide what the simulations are for, then test each option against that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST guidance is to tell staff that phishing exercises run at random and that results guide learning, not punishment. Announcing the program builds the trust that keeps staff reporting, and leaving dates unnamed keeps click rates honest, so secrecy adds nothing. A baseline round before any notice is the runner-up: it seems to measure staff as they really are, but it opens the program by tricking staff before they know one exists.

wrong_explanations.A: Telling only process owners leaves staff unaware, the flaw in the IT manager's plan; trust rests on staff knowing the program exists.
wrong_explanations.C: Naming each date lets staff watch for that day's email, so click rates stop showing how they handle phishing at other times.
wrong_explanations.D: A secret first round tricks staff before they know a program exists; random dates already keep results honest once it is announced.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps staff unaware, the plan's own flaw, and C names each date, which spoils the results; announcing the program with random timing avoids both.
Final two: B beats D because random timing already keeps results honest; a secret first round spends the trust simulations need in order to teach.
Exam cue: fair phishing simulations are announced as a program, not by date, and are used to teach, not to shame.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.7.2 (Experiential Learning: employees are told that phishing exercises run on a random basis and that results guide future learning, and the exercises are not punitive); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind)

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Moving an AI pilot into production
questions.question: An EV charging network's data science team built an AI pricing pilot, assessed its production risks, and chairs the stage-gate review that decides whether it goes live. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask the portfolio board to make the go-live decision
options.B: Add an independent reviewer to the team's gate panel
options.C: Get internal audit to sign off the pilot's results first
options.D: Record the gate's go-live outcome with the pricing risk owner

questions.key_concept: A stage gate needs a decider with no stake in passing; an AI pilot's move to production is decided by the body governing the investment.
questions.pre_read: Ask who makes the decision at the gate and what stake they have in its result.
questions.correct_explanation: The team that built and assessed the pricing pilot would be judging its own work at the gate it chairs. The go-live decision belongs with the portfolio board, which governs investments and weighs their value and risk, while the team presents its results and assessment. An independent reviewer on the panel is the runner-up: an outside view adds challenge, but the builders still chair the panel and decide.

wrong_explanations.B: An outside reviewer adds challenge, but the builders still chair the panel and make the decision; one voice does not remove their stake in passing.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives assurance on how decisions are made; signing off results would put it in management's role, and the builders would still decide.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the outcome with the risk owner notes a decision after the builders make it; the go-live decision stays with the team.

tips: Eliminate: C puts internal audit in management's approving role, and D records the team's decision after the fact; neither changes who decides at the gate.
Final two: A beats B because one outside reviewer on a panel the builders chair leaves the decision with them; the portfolio board did not build the pilot.

Exam cue: when the team that built something also decides whether it passes a gate, move the decision to the body that governs the investment; the risk owner still accepts or treats the residual risk.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Flags customers cannot see
questions.question: An HVAC installer refuses service plans to customers its billing system flags as late payers; refused customers are not told why and cannot dispute the flag. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Access to the flags limited to staff the data owner names
options.B: A review of the flags' accuracy by the billing data owner
options.C: A route for customers to view and correct their own flags
options.D: A privacy notice entry saying flags can affect service plans

questions.key_concept: When decisions about people rest on their personal data, privacy gives them a way to see that data and have errors corrected.
questions.pre_read: Note who is affected by the data and what they can and cannot do about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers are refused service on data they cannot see or challenge, so a wrong flag stays wrong and keeps costing them. Privacy principles give people a way to access and correct personal data used in decisions about them, which also catches errors case by case. An accuracy review by the data owner is the runner-up: it improves the flags overall, but a wrongly flagged customer still has no way to show the record is wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tighter access guards the flags against misuse, but the harm here comes from authorized use of data the customers cannot see or challenge.
wrong_explanations.B: A review by the firm helps overall accuracy, but customers still cannot see or challenge their own flags, so a wrong one keeps refusing them until it is found.
wrong_explanations.D: Telling customers that flags exist is transparency, not participation; they still cannot see their own flag or have it corrected.

tips: Eliminate: A guards the flags against misuse, a security answer, and D says flags exist without letting anyone check theirs; neither reaches a wrong flag.
Final two: C beats B because the stem's gap is that customers cannot see or challenge their flags; the firm's own review improves accuracy but gives a refused customer no route.
Exam cue: when decisions about people rest on data about them, look for a way for them to see and correct it; the organization's own checks do not replace that.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-18(4) (Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations | Individual Requests); NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 CT.PO-P3 (policies, processes and procedures for enabling individuals' data processing preferences and requests are established and in place)

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. An upgrade likely to delay surgeries
questions.question: A hospital instrument sterilization service's change board approved a weekday tracking-system upgrade that its impact assessment says will likely delay surgeries; no one outside IT was consulted. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Refer the upgrade's risk to the sterilization process owner
options.B: Require a tested back-out plan before the upgrade runs
options.C: Put the upgrade to a second vote of the change board
options.D: Schedule extra service desk staff for every hospital served

questions.key_concept: A change board approves a change; when its impact assessment shows likely harm to a business process, that process's owner decides on the risk.
questions.pre_read: Separate the decision to approve a change from the decision to accept its effect on the business.
questions.correct_explanation: The change board can approve a change, but likely surgery delays are a business risk, and the owner of the sterilization process carries that loss. That owner decides whether to accept the risk, move the upgrade or ask for more treatment. A tested back-out plan is the runner-up: it limits how long a failed upgrade lasts, but the assessment expects delays even from a working one, and accepting them is the owner's call.

wrong_explanations.B: A back-out plan shortens a failed upgrade, but the assessment expects delays even if it works; accepting them is the process owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: A second vote by the same board keeps the decision inside IT; the people who bear the surgery delays still have no say.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra desk staff speed up support, but the delays the assessment expects still fall on surgeries, and no business owner has weighed them.

tips: Eliminate: C asks the same board again, and D adds support staff; neither takes the risk to the person who bears the surgery delays.
Final two: A beats B because the assessment already expects delays; a back-out plan limits a failure, but accepting expected delays is the process owner's call.
Exam cue: the change board approves the change itself; when its impact assessment shows likely harm to a business process, that process's owner decides on the risk.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Security requirements before go-live
questions.question: A landscaping firm's booking app passed user acceptance testing, though no test checked its security requirements. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: A penetration test of the booking app
options.B: Go-live on the business owner's acceptance of the passed user tests
options.C: Monitoring of the live app against each security requirement
options.D: Test cases written to verify the app's security requirements

questions.key_concept: Security requirements are proven by tests written from them; user acceptance and penetration tests answer different questions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each kind of test is designed to show, and what the stem says is still unshown.
questions.correct_explanation: User acceptance testing shows the app does what the business needs; it does not show the security requirements were built. Test cases written from those requirements confirm each one before go-live, so the owner can accept the remaining risk knowing what it is. A penetration test is the runner-up: it looks for ways an attacker could break in, but it is not designed to confirm, one by one, that the agreed requirements are met.

wrong_explanations.A: A penetration test finds some exploitable flaws, but it is not designed to confirm that each agreed requirement, such as logging or role limits, is in place.
wrong_explanations.B: The user tests checked functions, not security; acceptance resting on them would accept risk from requirements no one has confirmed.
wrong_explanations.C: Checking requirements after go-live finds gaps once customers' data is already exposed; the time to confirm them is before launch.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts risk on user tests that never checked security, and C checks the requirements after launch; both leave them unconfirmed when it matters.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is unverified requirements; a penetration test hunts for exploitable flaws but does not confirm each requirement was built.
Exam cue: requirements are proven by tests written from them; other tests, however good, answer a different question.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Retired recipes in a wide-open archive
questions.question: A confectioner moves retired recipes, classified restricted, to an archive tier every IT employee can read; many share formulations with current best sellers. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A lower class for archived recipes, set by the data owner
options.B: The restricted class's handling rules, with access the data owner approves
options.C: Alerts on unusual downloads of restricted recipes from the archive
options.D: A second copy of the archive kept with another storage provider

questions.key_concept: Data keeps its class and handling rules when it moves to an archive; a class falls when sensitivity falls, not when data is retired.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the moved data still reveals, then match its protection to that.
questions.correct_explanation: A class sets handling rules wherever the data sits, and moving recipes to an archive does not change what they reveal. Many still share formulations with current best sellers, so they stay restricted, and the archive must apply that class's rules, such as access limited to people the data owner approves. A lower class is the runner-up: the owner can reclassify data whose sensitivity has fallen, but these formulations are as sensitive as before.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner can lower a class when sensitivity falls, but these recipes still reveal how current best sellers are made, so a lower class would misstate them.
wrong_explanations.C: Alerts may spot a bulk download once it starts, but every IT employee could still read the recipes; the restricted rules are not applied.
wrong_explanations.D: A second copy protects against losing the archive, but the risk here is who can read it; another copy is one more place to protect.

tips: Eliminate: C watches for misuse of access that should not exist, and D guards against loss when the risk is exposure; neither applies the recipes' class.
Final two: B beats A because many archived recipes still reveal current products; a class falls when sensitivity falls, not when data moves to an archive.
Exam cue: data keeps its class, and the class's handling rules, when it is moved, copied or archived; ask what it still reveals before lowering it.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Wrong answers from an AI help assistant
questions.question: A web hosting firm's AI help assistant, up all quarter, told customers to delete DNS records they needed; IT operations, which runs it, treats only outages as incidents. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Retrain the assistant on DNS articles IT operations has checked
options.B: Report the share of unhelpful chats beside incident counts
options.C: Send a copy of each customer complaint to the support owner
options.D: Have IT operations add harmful answers to its incident criteria

questions.key_concept: Harmful AI outputs can be incidents even while the service is up, so the incident criteria must include them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens today when the assistant gives a harmful answer, and who would ever act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A service can be up and still harm its users; an assistant giving advice that breaks customers' sites is failing, so its harmful answers are incidents. With them in IT operations' incident criteria, each is logged, triaged by impact, contained and traced to its cause. Retraining is the runner-up: it targets the DNS answers seen so far, but their cause is unknown, and the next harmful answer would still go unhandled.

wrong_explanations.A: Retraining aims at the answers already seen before their cause is known, and the next harmful answer, on DNS or anything else, would still go unlogged and unhandled.
wrong_explanations.B: An unhelpful-chat share measures satisfaction, not harm; a harmful answer can look helpful, and reporting a share gets no single answer triaged or contained.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying complaints keeps the support owner informed, but it starts no triage, containment or cause analysis; the harmful answers stay outside incident handling.

tips: Eliminate: B reports satisfaction rather than harm, and C passes complaints to the support owner without starting any response; neither gets a harmful answer handled.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is that harmful answers never enter incident handling; retraining before the cause is known fixes, at best, the cases already seen.
Exam cue: an incident includes a drop in service quality that harms users, not only an outage; when harmful AI output misses the incident criteria, widen them.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Replication lag against the RPO
questions.question: A blood bank's unit-tracking database replicates to a second site; IT reports its five-minute RPO met because lag averages 40 seconds, though lag hit three hours at month-end. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Alerts to the system owner when lag passes the RPO
options.B: Replication capacity that keeps lag within the RPO at peak
options.C: Restore tests of the replica that the system owner reviews
options.D: Immutable backups kept beside the replicated database

questions.key_concept: An RPO caps data loss at every moment, so replication must stay within it at peak load, not only on average.
questions.pre_read: Compare the target with every figure in the stem before choosing a fix.
questions.correct_explanation: An RPO is the most data the business can afford to lose, so it must hold at the worst moment, not on average. With lag at three hours at month-end, a site loss then would wipe out hours of blood-unit records, so replication must stay within five minutes at peak. Alerts to the system owner are the runner-up: they show the breach as it happens, but records written during the lag would still be lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Alerts make the breach visible as it happens, but they do not shorten the lag; a site loss at month-end would still lose hours of records.
wrong_explanations.C: A restore test shows the replica can be brought back and how current it was on test day, not at month-end peaks; the lag stays as it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Immutable backups protect against corruption and ransomware, but they do not bring the replica up to date; a month-end failure still loses the lagged records.

tips: Eliminate: C tests whether the replica restores, not how current it is, and D adds protected copies against corruption; neither shortens the lag behind the RPO.
Final two: B beats A because an RPO is a ceiling on data loss; alerts report the breach while records are being lost, and capacity sized for the peak is what keeps lag inside it.
Exam cue: judge an RPO or RTO against the worst credible case the business faces, not the average; averages hide the moments when the target fails.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Chip origin records on a shared ledger
questions.question: A circuit board maker plans to stop authenticity tests on incoming chips once its suppliers record each lot's origin on an industry blockchain, which the vendor calls tamper-proof. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Rival board makers reading suppliers' lot data on the ledger
options.B: Slower goods receipt while each lot is matched to the ledger
options.C: Counterfeit chip lots entered on the ledger as genuine parts
options.D: Chip lot histories lost if the ledger platform's vendor fails

questions.key_concept: A blockchain makes changes to entries evident but cannot prove they were true, so it cannot replace a check on the physical goods.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the new technology actually proves, and what the dropped control used to check.
questions.correct_explanation: A blockchain makes later changes to an entry evident; it cannot show the entry was true. Once the authenticity tests stop, a counterfeit lot recorded as genuine, by a supplier who was fooled or dishonest, would go straight into the maker's boards. Rivals reading lot data is the runner-up: shared ledgers can expose business data, but that harm is smaller than fake chips reaching customers' products unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Shared ledgers can expose business data, so access settings matter, but leaked lot details do less harm than counterfeit chips built into customers' boards.
wrong_explanations.B: Slower receipt is an efficiency cost the maker can measure and manage; it does not let a single bad chip through.
wrong_explanations.D: A failed vendor would cost lot history, a loss the maker can rebuild from supplier records; counterfeit chips passing untested would reach products and customers.

tips: Eliminate: B is an efficiency cost and D a vendor exit risk; neither lets a bad chip into a board.
Final two: C beats A because the plan drops the check on the chips themselves; a ledger shows whether records changed, not whether they were true, and exposed lot data is a smaller harm.
Exam cue: a tamper-evident record proves nothing about what was entered; before a new technology replaces a control, ask what the old control checked that the technology cannot.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8202 Section 7.3 (Beyond the Digital: a blockchain may have no way to tell whether recorded input reflects real-world events, and people can record false information)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Deal makers and the appetite statement
questions.question: A vocational college's department heads sign software and partner deals but have never seen the board's risk appetite statement; two deals sent student records to unvetted firms. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Disciplinary warnings for the two heads who signed the deals
options.B: Publication of the appetite statement on the staff intranet
options.C: A refresher security course for every member of staff
options.D: Briefings for the heads on applying the appetite to deals

questions.key_concept: People who make risk decisions need to know how the risk appetite applies to their own choices, not just that a statement exists.
questions.pre_read: Look at who is making the risky decisions and what they were missing when they made them.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness has to reach the people making risk decisions in terms they can use. Department heads sign deals that take on risk, so they need to see how the board's appetite applies to choices such as sharing student records; that shapes all their future deals, not just these two. Publishing the statement is the runner-up: heads could then read it, but a board-level statement alone does not show them which deals cross the line.

wrong_explanations.A: Warnings punish two people for a gap the college created by never showing them the appetite; the next head would make the same call, and blame discourages reporting.
wrong_explanations.B: Posting the statement lets heads read it, but board-level wording does not show a head which software or partner deals fall outside it.
wrong_explanations.C: A general security course covers neither the board's appetite nor the deal decisions heads make; it trains everyone and changes none of those choices.

tips: Eliminate: A blames two heads for a gap in what they were shown, and C gives every member of staff a general course that does not cover the appetite or their deals.
Final two: D beats B because the heads need to apply the appetite, not just see it; a posted board statement leaves each of them guessing what it means for a deal.
Exam cue: risk awareness for decision makers means showing them how the appetite applies to the choices they make; publishing a statement is not the same as being understood.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-02 (individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind)

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Data gathered before its uses are set
questions.question: A student housing provider's tenant app will log door entries and phone locations, with uses to be decided after launch. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encryption of the app's logged data at rest and in transit
options.B: Purposes for the data, set by the data owner before collection
options.C: Tenants' consent to the app's data collection, given at sign-up
options.D: Access to the logs limited to staff whom the data owner names

questions.key_concept: The purpose for personal data is set before it is collected; consent, minimization, retention and access rules all follow from it.
questions.pre_read: Put the options in the order they would happen, then apply the priority word.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy starts with purpose: an organization decides why it needs personal data before collecting it, and that purpose then limits what is collected, how long it is kept and who may use it. Here the data owner should set the purposes before launch. Tenants' consent is the runner-up: consent counts only when people know what they are agreeing to, and with uses undecided, tenants would be agreeing to nothing specific.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects the logs from outsiders but says nothing about why they are collected or how staff may use them; privacy asks more than security does.
wrong_explanations.C: Consent needs a stated purpose to be informed; asking tenants to agree before any use is decided gives them nothing specific to agree to.
wrong_explanations.D: Access limits control who sees the logs, not whether entries and locations should be gathered; with no purpose set, no one can say who needs them.

tips: Eliminate: A and D are security controls that keep the logs from the wrong people; privacy first asks why the app gathers entries and locations, and neither answers that.
Final two: B beats C because consent is valid only for a purpose people are told; with uses still undecided, there is nothing yet to consent to.
Exam cue: when data would be collected first and its uses decided later, set the purpose first; consent, minimization, retention and access all depend on it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (purpose limitation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Generative AI services the standards do not cover
questions.question: A mobile network operator's architecture standards say nothing about generative AI services, and five teams have each licensed a different chatbot service for their own work. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Generative AI patterns approved through the architecture review board
options.B: Architecture exceptions, with owners, recorded for the five services
options.C: A block on generative AI services at the network edge
options.D: Shadow AI awareness sessions for staff in the five teams

questions.key_concept: When architecture standards are silent on a technology teams are adopting, EA governance adds approved patterns so every team has a vetted route.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the architecture standards say about this technology and how many teams have already acted on their own.
questions.correct_explanation: The teams broke no rule: the architecture has none for generative AI, so each team chose its own service. Patterns approved through the architecture review board set the services, data handling and integration conditions any team can use, and the five services are then checked against them. Recording exceptions is the runner-up: an exception marks a departure from a standard, and with none in place, the next team would face the same gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Exceptions suit a departure from an existing standard; none exists here, so five exceptions would describe today's services and leave the next team with no approved route.
wrong_explanations.C: Blocking the services at the network edge bans a technology by reflex, gives up its value and pushes staff toward personal accounts the operator cannot see.
wrong_explanations.D: Awareness sessions warn staff about unapproved AI, but these teams licensed services openly because no standard told them what to use; the gap sits in the architecture.

tips: Eliminate: C bans a technology by reflex instead of judging its risk, and D trains staff when the teams acted openly because the architecture gave them no approved route.
Final two: A beats B because an exception records a departure from a standard, and the standards say nothing on generative AI; approved patterns give every team a vetted path.
Exam cue: when teams adopt a technology the architecture standards do not cover, close the gap in the standards through EA governance; one exception per team leaves the next team stuck.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-7 (Enterprise Architecture); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 6.1 (policies and procedures address AI risks from third-party entities, including infringement of a third party's intellectual property or other rights)

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). A trade-show demo that went live
questions.question: An appliance maker's marketing team built a recipe app outside the SDLC as a trade-show demo, then published it; it now holds 40,000 customer accounts. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: An SDLC exemption for the demo, approved by its business owner
options.B: Support for the app handed over from marketing to IT operations
options.C: The live app taken through the formal design and test gates
options.D: Multifactor sign-in added to the app's customer accounts

questions.key_concept: A demo or prototype that becomes a live system goes through the SDLC gates it skipped before its controls are chosen.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the app was built as, what it is now and which steps it missed on the way.
questions.correct_explanation: A demo became a live system holding 40,000 customers' accounts without the design and test gates that set its security requirements and check them. Taking it through those gates now assesses its risks, sets requirements and tests the app, with its business owner deciding on what remains. Adding multifactor sign-in is the runner-up: it may prove to be one of the right controls, but it is chosen before anyone knows the app's risks.

wrong_explanations.A: An exemption keeps a live app holding 40,000 customers' accounts outside the gates; how it started does not change its untested design.
wrong_explanations.B: IT operations can run the app day to day, but running it neither assesses nor tests its design; the gates it skipped stay skipped.
wrong_explanations.D: Multifactor sign-in may suit the accounts, but it is one control picked before the app's risks are known; flaws in an untested design stay open.

tips: Eliminate: A exempts the app as a demo without changing its risk, and B moves day-to-day running to IT operations, which neither assesses nor tests the design.
Final two: C beats D because the gates find what the app needs before controls are chosen; multifactor sign-in is one guess at a control for an app nobody has assessed.
Exam cue: when a demo, prototype or trial build becomes a live system, it enters the SDLC gates it skipped; how it started does not exempt it from assessment and testing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-3 (System Development Life Cycle); NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task P-14 (Risk Assessment for the System: conduct a system-level risk assessment from initiation and update it on an ongoing basis)

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Personal data left in resold trade-ins
questions.question: A car dealer resold a trade-in whose dashboard screen still held the seller's contacts and home address; its pre-sale inspection covers only mechanical faults. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A recorded wipe of personal data in the resale process
options.B: A one-time wipe of stored data from every used car in stock
options.C: A trade-in form asking sellers to clear their data before resale
options.D: A confidentiality clause in the buyer's sale contract

questions.key_concept: Storage in any device the organization releases, such as a resold car, is wiped and recorded as a step in the release process.
questions.pre_read: Note where the personal data was stored and what the dealer checks before a car is sold.
questions.correct_explanation: Each trade-in leaves the dealer's control at resale, so personal data stored in it must be removed first, as with any device the dealer releases. A recorded wipe in the resale process makes that happen for every car and leaves evidence it was done. A trade-in form asking sellers to clear their data is the runner-up: it helps, but the dealer releases the car and cannot rely on sellers remembering or knowing how.

wrong_explanations.B: Clearing the cars in stock fixes today's lot, but trade-ins keep arriving with sellers' data; with no step in the resale process, the next sale repeats it.
wrong_explanations.C: Asking sellers helps, but some will forget or not know how; the dealer is the one releasing the car, so the task cannot rest on sellers.
wrong_explanations.D: A clause tells buyers to keep found data private, but the data still reaches them; contract terms govern use after disclosure, not the disclosure itself.

tips: Eliminate: B cleans the cars in stock today but not the trade-ins still to come, and D binds buyers by contract after the data has already reached them.
Final two: A beats C because the dealer releases the car and so must clear it; a request to sellers moves the task to people the dealer cannot check.
Exam cue: any device that stores personal data, not only computers, needs a recorded wipe before it leaves the organization's control; build the step into the release process.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. An approved fix that never reached the backlog
questions.question: A dredging contractor's risk owner approved a survey-platform access fix for the platform's Agile team to build; four sprints on, the team's backlog holds no item for it. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Have the product owner add the fix to the definition of done
options.B: Escalate the missing backlog item to the enterprise risk committee
options.C: Seek portfolio board funding for a separate access fix project
options.D: Ask the product owner to put the fix into the team's backlog

questions.key_concept: Agile teams build what their backlog holds, so an approved risk response must become a backlog item before it can be scheduled.
questions.pre_read: Note how this team chooses its work and where the approved fix has been recorded so far.
questions.correct_explanation: An Agile team builds from its backlog, so an approved response that never enters it is not scheduled, however long it waits. Asking the product owner, who orders the backlog, to add the fix as an item puts it where sprint work is chosen. Escalating to the risk committee is the runner-up: it adds pressure, but the risk owner has already decided, and the fix still has no place in any sprint.

wrong_explanations.A: The definition of done lists criteria an item must meet before it counts as finished; a one-off fix is work to schedule as a backlog item, not a criterion.
wrong_explanations.B: Escalation adds pressure, but the risk owner has already decided; the committee has nothing to decide, and the fix stays out of sprints while it is missing from the backlog.
wrong_explanations.C: The fix is approved and has a team to build it; a separately funded project adds a new investment decision and delay where one backlog item is needed.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses the definition of done, which sets criteria for finished work, with the backlog, and C sends an approved fix with a team to a new funding decision.
Final two: D beats B because the fix stalls for want of a backlog item, and the product owner can add it there; escalation leaves that cause in place.
Exam cue: in Agile delivery, an approved risk response is built only once it is a backlog item; when one never reached the backlog, have it entered before escalating any delay.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Duties one administrator cannot split
questions.question: A language school's only office administrator issues student refunds and also reconciles the bank account the refunds are paid from. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Least-privilege refund rights for the administrator, set by the system owner
options.B: The director's review of refund records and bank reconciliations
options.C: A refund limit, with larger refunds approved by the director
options.D: Fidelity insurance the business owner buys against staff fraud

questions.key_concept: Where conflicting duties cannot be split, an independent review acts as a compensating control for the missing separation.
questions.pre_read: Name the two duties one person holds and what the second duty could hide about the first.
questions.correct_explanation: Issuing refunds and reconciling the account they leave from are conflicting duties: the administrator could pay a false refund and hide it in the reconciliation. With one administrator the duties cannot be split, so the director's independent review of refund records and reconciliations acts as the compensating control. A refund limit is the runner-up: it stops large single refunds, but small false ones still pass and the same person reconciles them.

wrong_explanations.A: Least privilege trims rights the job does not need, but this job needs both duties; the danger is one person holding the conflicting pair, which it does not address.
wrong_explanations.C: A limit with director approval stops large single refunds, but false refunds under the limit still pass, and the administrator who issues them also reconciles them.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance can repay a fraud loss once it is found, but it neither prevents nor detects false refunds; with no review, a loss may never come to light.

tips: Eliminate: A applies least privilege, which judges rights one at a time, to a conflict between two needed duties, and D insures against losses without preventing or detecting any.
Final two: B beats C because an independent review covers small refunds and the reconciliation that could hide them; a limit checks only the large ones.
Exam cue: when a small team cannot split conflicting duties, look for an independent review that supplies the missing second person; the risk owner then accepts what remains.
